title: The numbers behind NI's 158 Commonwealth Games medals
description: As the Games in Glasgow come to a close, BBC Sport NI looks at the numbers behind Northern Ireland's 158 Commonwealth Games medals.
fullText:
With 16 medals in Glasgow, Team Northern Ireland surpassed the landmark of 150 medals at the Commonwealth Games.

It has been a successful games for Northern Ireland athletes, and a tally of three golds, four silvers and nine bronze medals in Glasgow to take the overall tally to 158 medals.

It is the second-highest number of medals for Northern Ireland in the history of the Commonwealth Games.

Kate O'Connor was dominant in the heptathlon and boxer Jon McConnell claimed a famous gold medal, while the Games ended with Gary Kelly and Adam McKeown winning the men's pars final in bowls.

There was also success in the ring with further six medals and another four in the swimming pool.

But what are the numbers behind Northern Ireland's success at the Games? Let's break it down.

O'Connor wins NI's first gold medal in heptathlon

Wiffen rallies for silver as McCartney claims bronze

McConnell takes gold as Walsh and Rock claim silver

Why the Commonwealth Games are important to NI athletes

Northern Ireland have competed in all but two Commonwealth Games.

The first edition in 1930, when it was known as the Empire Games, athletes from Northern Ireland participated in Ontario as Ireland, and claimed a silver medal through Bill Britton in the hammer throw, but in this article we will focus on medals won as Team Northern Ireland.

The first medals as Northern Ireland came in 1934 in London, when the men's fours team claimed a silver in bowls, while William Duncan and Jimmy Magill won boxing bronze medals.

After a medal-less 1938 Games and no Northern Ireland representatives in Auckland when the Games resumed in 1950 after the end of the World War Two, the first two gold medals arrived in Vancouver in 1954 - the first year it was known as the Empire and Commonwealth Games.

Thelma Hopkins won the high jump, while William Rosbotham and Percy Watson - remarkably also one of the 1934 silver medallists - won the men's pairs in bowls.

Edinburgh has been a productive city for Northern Ireland in the Commonwealths, and 1970 brought two gold medals for Dame Mary Peters, in the pentathlon and shot put, while Mike Bull took gold in the pole vault.

Sixteen years later, Northern Ireland had their most successful Games up to that point with 15 medals.

Phil Beattie's 400m hurdles win and Freda Elliott and Margaret Johnston's women's pairs triumph in the bowls were the only two golds, but four silvers and nine bronze medals made it NI's most fruitful Games yet.

The 1994 Commonwealths in Victoria set a new Northern Ireland record for the number of gold medals at a single competition with five, as Johnston claimed a singles title, Neil Sinclair and Jimmy Webb won gold in the ring, while David Calvert and the duo of Tom Hewitt and Samuel Allen were successful in shooting.

Calvert would strike again four years later with two golds, one of which came in the pairs event with Martin Millar, and another individual double followed in 2002 in Manchester.

The 2010 Games in Dehli are remembered for a hat-trick of boxing golds as Michael Conlan, Paddy Barnes and Eamonn O'Kane all won, and the former pair became double Commonwealth champions in Glasgow four years later.

Rhys McClenaghan's triumph on the Gold Coast in 2018 was a first gymnastics medal for Northern Ireland and seven silver medals plus four bronze matched the tally of 12 medals from Glasgow.

But it was in 2022 in Birmingham when Northern Ireland had, by some distance, their most successful Games to date with seven gold medals, seven silvers and four bronze.

Aidan and Michaela Walsh, Jude Gallagher, Dylan Eagleson and Amy Broadhurst all won golds in boxing, while Bethany Firth came out on top in the women's 200m S14 and the men's four quartet of Martin McHugh, Ian McClure, Sam Barkley and Adam McKeown were triumphant in bowls.

There were also notable silvers for Daniel Wiffen and McClenaghan, who both would go on to become Olympic champions two years later, while Ciara Mageean and O'Connor, who won NI's first gold in 2026, finished second in the 1500m and heptathlon respectively.

Jon McConnell added to O'Connor's success in Glasgow with a gold in the ring, and the duo of Kelly and McKeown ended NI's Games on a high with victory in the men's pairs final.

In terms of a number of gold medals and an overall tally, boxing is the most successful sport for athletes from Northern Ireland - and by some margin.

Of the 18 gold medals won in the sport, there have been a number of notable names who went on to have distinguished careers.

Barry McGuigan won gold in Edmonton in 1978, Wayne McCullough was Commonwealth champion in 1990, while Barnes is the only boxer to win consecutive gold medals.

The first gold for a NI boxer came in 1958 in Cardiff through Terry Milligan, and it is fitting the landmark 150th medal also came in the ring with a flurry of medals on Friday.

Such has been the success of NI boxers, they have won 49% of all Commonwealth medals.

Bowls is next in line with another successful Games, with Kelly winning bronze in the singles before he pairs gold with McKeown, while Chloe Wilson and Shauna O'Neill claimed bronze in the women's competition.

That takes bowls' tally to 25 overall, six of which are gold.

Neil Booth and Kelly have four medals to his name, while Margaret Johnston and Ian McClure each have two golds and a bronze to their name.

Lady Peters leads the athletics tally with her three gold medals and a silver, and O'Connor's gold in Glasgow was the first in a multi-event since the 1972 Olympic champion, and the first athletics gold since Beattie in 1986.

Northern Ireland have only won a gold medal in six sports, and McClenaghan in 2018 and Firth's success four years ago are the only time in their respective events.

There have been three sports where Northern Ireland has one solitary medal - with Ivan Weir winning middleweight bronze in wrestling in 1978, Janet Yates claimed silver four years later in archery and Chloe McCombe, along with guide Catherine Sands, in the para-triathlon in Birmingham in 2022.

There have also been eight judo medals - two of which came from Joshua Green and Rachael Hawkes in Glasgow - and four in cycling, but none have been gold.

Along with McCombe, Firth and swimmer Barry McClements are the other para-athletes who have won medals for Northern Ireland.

Shooter David Calvert is the most successful athlete from Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, with eight medals - four of which were gold.

Calvert's first medal came at the 1982 Games in Brisbane alongside Hazel Mackintosh in the full bore rifle pairs.

His first gold came in Victoria in 1994 in same discipline and his last was a bronze medal in Delhi in 2010 aged 59, which made him the oldest NI athlete to medal.

Six athletes from Northern Ireland have won four medals each.

Shooter Martin Millar won his two gold medals alongside Calvert, and has two bronze medals to his name.

Lady Mary Peters and Mike Bull both won silver for their first Games medals in 1966, in the shot put and pole vault respectively.

Peters won a shot put and pentathlon double in 1970 - the latter of which she would win again four years later - while Bull was first in the decathlon in 1974 and also added another gold and silver to his pole vault tally.

Michaela Walsh is the first boxer to win four medals for Northern Ireland. She won gold in 2022 to add to her silvers in 2014 and 2018, and claimed a third silver in Glasgow on Saturday.

After his gold on Sunday, Kelly joins fellow bowler Neil Booth on a quartet of Commonwealth medals.

title: From European hopes to relegation form - will Moyes reignite Everton?
description: Everton competed for the European places before falling away last season. BBC Sport examines whether David Moyes is the right man to turn them around this term.
fullText:
For much of last season, Everton were looking up.

Loan signing Jack Grealish proved to be an instant hit. Fellow new arrival Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was a reliable matchwinner. Strikers Thierno Barry and Beto had shrugged off early-season struggles to start scoring goals.

A 3-0 triumph against Chelsea on 21 March put Everton eighth in the Premier League, just three points off the Champions League places with seven games left.

Supporters were dreaming big. Instead, the team imploded.

Everton failed to win any of their remaining matches - the longest run without a victory since David Moyes returned for a second spell in charge of the Toffees in 2025.

A 2-2 draw at Brentford on 11 April sparked a decline in form over the remainder of the campaign that ranked Everton in the bottom three during that period.

They were one of only three teams to fail to win a match during this spell, along with relegated Burnley and Wolves.

Despite the drop off, Everton retained hopes of European football when they faced Sunderland in their final home match of 2025-26.

In his program notes, Everton CEO Angus Kinnear declared that he was "happily dissatisfied" with the campaign - an odd turn of phrase at a confusing moment that quickly soured after a 3-1 defeat.

Promoted Sunderland would go on to finish seventh and secure European football for the first time in 53 years.

The irony for Moyes is that Everton have finished 13th in both seasons since his return, but to very different receptions.

When he rejoined the club 18 months ago, the Toffees were one point above the relegation zone. They would go on to finish 23 points clear of the bottom three.

Everton then spent £97m before the 2025-26 campaign - a club record net outlay in a summer transfer window - to repeat the same finish having accrued one more point.

Former Everton midfielder Leon Osman believes after a chaotic period of financial breaches, points deductions and relegation battles, successive mid-table finishes demonstrate progress.

"When David Moyes first came in, we flew out the blocks and had a great start," he said. "That continued for well over a year before the first sort of low period, which was the end of last season.

"I still feel that we made progress last season, which is what we wanted, along with stability."

Moyes, 63, has spoken of the challenge of keeping up with the biggest spenders in the Premier League, with Everton ranking 15th of the current top-flight teams for net spend over the past five years.

Bournemouth, however, spent the least of any Premier League team last summer, making a profit of £81m from player sales, and still finished seven places higher in sixth. Brighton made a profit of £41m and finished eighth.

Moving to the state-of-the-art Hill Dickinson Stadium promised a new dawn but Everton's points-per-game tally of 1.2 at home last season was the lowest by any team to start life in a new stadium in the Premier League in the competition's history - in stark comparison to strong away form which ranked the Toffees in the top seven.

Osman believes Bournemouth and Brighton are "further along in their development" than an Everton side still adjusting to new surroundings after a tumultuous period, and that the loss of Grealish to injury in January was key.

Everton's win rate dropped from 45% and 1.6 points per game with Grealish to 22% and one point per game without him.

"David Moyes is an intense manager and by the end of the season, a small squad couldn't quite last," said the 45-year-old.

"Changes take time. No one is thinking about relegation which shows you what Moyes has done. He's got 12 months remaining and I'd expect him to see that out."

While the success of Bournemouth and Brighton has been built on impressive recruitment models, Everton's transfer strategy remains a work in progress.

Under previous owner Farhad Moshiri, eight players signed for at least £20m left for nothing.

Following several years of limited spending, nine players were then recruited by the Friedkin Group last summer, although a focus on youth has yet to bear fruit.

Grealish and Dewsbury-Hall have been successful but 20-year-old winger Tyler Dibling has started only six matches after costing £35m from Southampton.

Young left-back Adam Aznou, who joined from Bayern Munich last summer, is still awaiting his Premier League debut.

Striker Barry, 23, won more aerial duels than any other player in his first Premier League campaign but was inconsistent in front of goal.

Midfielder Merlin Rohl, 24, initially struggled for game time before impressing over four starts in May.

BBC Radio Merseyside reporter Giulia Bould says the influential Grealish is set to re-sign on loan towards the end of this window as he continues to rehabilitate from a stress fracture to his foot.

His wages, however, are expected to stick at about £200,000 per week.

Iliman Ndiaye, meanwhile, has been linked with a move to Saudia Arabia.

"I'd welcome Grealish back but only at a price that suits Everton," says Osman, who was given his Everton debut by Moyes during the manager's first spell in charge in 2003.

"Ndiaye, I'd hate to lose him. There may come a point that the price is right and Everton can reinvest in two or three players but I think they should do everything they can to keep him."

Losing elite quality without sensible reinvestment is not something Everton can afford with one of the Premier League's smaller squads.

Moyes used just 22 players in the top flight in 2025-26 - the lowest of any side - while 128 substitutions were at least six fewer than any other manager.

Everton continue to focus a significant slice of their recruitment on development players.

Central midfielder Hayden Hackney, 24, joined from Middlesbrough for £16.5m in July along with 20-year-old winger Tyrique George, who was signed from Chelsea for £18m having spent the second half of last season on loan at Everton.

The more experienced Celtic defender Alistair Johnston is the latest player linked with solving the problem position at right-back, while 32-year-old Arsenal midfielder Christian Norgaard is reportedly an imminent arrival.

The average age of signings in Moyes' second spell is under 24, including three players aged 20 or younger.

But players aged 21 or under featured for 1,088 minutes for the club last season, ranking Everton only 17th in the Premier League.

The departures of Seamus Coleman and Idrissa Gueye deprive Everton of more than 600 Premier League appearances - explaining the interest in Norgaard - while key midfielder James Garner is set to miss the start of the season following groin surgery.

As things stand, it leaves Moyes in the paradoxical position of being potentially reliant on younger players he appears more reluctant to trust.

"They need to show they're capable and deserve to play," added Osman.

"I'm hoping that a year in, understanding the demands that are required, players like Dibling and George will make that progression and then suddenly our squad looks more trustworthy."

title: Gang of men hurl racist abuse at takeaway owner before violent attack
description: The BBC understands police are treating the attack in Falkirk last month as a hate crime.
fullText:
A business owner has said that a group of men hurled racist abuse at him before punching him and smashing his head into a wall in the street in Falkirk.

Dr Zohaib Arshad said the group approached him on Grahams Road last month when he was visiting one of his takeaway shops and asked him when he was "leaving the country" before launching the unprovoked attack.

The 39-year-old, who practised as a vet in Pakistan, patched himself up with glue stitches rather than wait at A&E. He said his children are now fearful of being attacked in school.

BBC Scotland understands the police are treating the incident as a hate crime.

A spokesperson for the force said inquiries into the attack are ongoing.

Arshad stood as an Alba Party candidate for Falkirk at the 2024 General Election and is now a member of the SNP.

His political connections have resulted in the issue being brought to the attention of the Scottish Parliament - however he fears it would have gone unnoticed had he been any other member of the public.

More stories from Tayside and Central

Listen to news from Tayside and Central on BBC Sounds

Arshad said he had just parked his car and was walking to one of his shops on the evening of Monday 20 July.

He said: "Two or three guys approached me and said 'when are you leaving the country by the way?'"

The businessman said he tried to walk away but one of the group banged his head into the wall.

"I had blood all over my face and in my eyes and when I was cleaning up the blood from my eyes one of the guys punched me on my head a few times," he said.

He told how he then ended up in a fight with one of the men as he tried to defend himself, and that the man threatened to stab him.

Despite there being lots of people around, he said nobody came to his assistance.

"Everybody got their phone at that time instead of helping me or helping that guy to take the situation out. Everybody was just filming us," he said.

The 39-year-old said that after calling the police it took 45 minutes for officers to arrive, by which time the men had left the scene.

When Arshad called for an ambulance, he claims he was told to make his own way to A&E.

"I called A&E and A&E said oh it's 14 hours to get the stitches," he said.

He feared that leaving the wound untreated for that long would leave him with a worse scar, so called some of his friends who work in medicine to see if they had "glue stitches at home" and stitched the wound up in "the back of the shop".

Following the attack, Arshad said his family are "terrified" and he is being "much more vigilant".

"My wee boy, he's nine and said 'dad, if I go to school, can they do it to me as well?'"

He added that despite his wife and his mother urging him to move to France where he lived previously, he has no plans to leave Scotland.

"We cannot leave anything just because of one bad person - defeat is not an option," he said.

It comes at a time of heightened tension over the issue of immigration in Scotland.

Police made several arrests in the opening weekend of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow after masked demonstrators rampaged through the city and targeted people for the colour of their skin.

Earlier in the day a peaceful anti-racism protest had been taking place at Glasgow Green before anti-immigration protesters arrived at the same location - police estimated 1,700 people had attended.

Later that day a group marching through the city shouted racist abuse and hurled a traffic cone at a delivery driver who was picking up an order.

A video of the attack on Muhammad Jawad Yaqoob circulated on social media - it shows a number of young men shouting "get them out" before one throws the orange cone. They cheer as Yaquoob runs away from them into a nearby restaurant.

Police Scotland said it was investigating the incident.

title: What happened to star signings your club never made?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at some star players who were close to moving to the Premier League, only for the deals to fall through.
fullText:
Fans always get excited when the transfer window comes around.

Your team is linked with a big-name signing and you start to dream they could be the ones to lead your club to glory.

Tottenham fans might have felt this way a few years ago when they were strongly linked with a young, prolific striker from Nigeria by the name of Gift Orban.

They had every reason, on paper at least, to be excited.

In the summer of 2023, Orban, then 21, was regarded as one of the hottest prospects in the game.

After scoring 16 goals in 22 games for Norwegian top-flight side Stabaek, he moved to Belgian side Gent and continued his impressive goalscoring record, netting 20 times in 22 matches.

In a wild four-day period in March 2023, he scored seven goals in two matches. He got four in a 6–2 away league win over Zulte Waregem, becoming the first Gent player with a four-goal haul in one game in the 21st Century.

He then followed up with a quick-fire hat-trick in a 4–1 away victory over Istanbul Basaksehir in the Conference League last 16.

That hat-trick was completed within three minutes and 25 seconds, at the time a record in Uefa club competitions.

With England captain Harry Kane set to join Bayern Munich later that summer, Tottenham needed a striker.

Orban was even touted in the BBC Gossip Column as the club's Kane replacement. The headline of a follow-up story read: "Could Orban be a global star?"

However, Spurs, with new boss Ange Postecoglou recently appointed, stalled at the £25m fee and the move collapsed.

In the three years since, Orban has had four clubs, most recently joining newly-promoted Turkish top-flight side Amedspor on loan last week.

He has struggled to regain his form with only three goals for Gent in 2023-24, three for French side Lyon and four for Bundesliga outfit Hoffenheim, although he scored seven times in Serie A on loan at Verona last season.

While his career is yet to reach the heights it once promised, other missed transfer targets have had rather different outcomes...

In January 2009, newly-rich Manchester City were looking to spend a bit of their bulging bank balance to sign Brazilian playmaker Kaka.

AC Milan and Kaka's heads were turned by City's staggering £108m offer, which would have been more than double the world record transfer at the time.

One City fan was so sure the deal would be done that he apparently got the playmaker's name tattooed on his chest., external

However, in the end, the 2007 Ballon d'Or winner decided the timing wasn't right and turned down the chance to move to Manchester.

Kaka did make a world-record move later in 2009, joining Real Madrid for £56m six months later.

He won the Spanish Cup in 2011 and La Liga the following year before one season back at AC Milan.

He then spent three years at Major League Soccer side Orlando City before ending his playing career back in his homeland with Sao Paulo.

In 2004, Bolton Wanderers were flying high, with dreams of Europe.

Manager Sam Allardyce went big, with an enquiry for 32-year-old Brazilian World Cup winner Rivaldo, who had been frozen out at AC Milan.

Rivaldo himself made a statement, saying: "I want the challenge of trying to get Bolton into Europe for the first time in their history. It is an exciting time."

In the end, he had a change of heart and went to Greek side Olympiakos instead, where he stayed for three seasons.

Bolton finished that 2004-05 campaign in sixth - tied on points with Liverpool and just three points off the top four. That earned them a place in Uefa Cup qualifying, and they went on to reach the last 32.

After Olympiakos, Rivaldo had spells with AEK Athens, then in Uzbekistan and Angola before returning to Brazil.

In 1995, Blackburn Rovers had just won the Premier League title and turned down the chance to sign a young French midfielder, Zinedine Zidane from Bordeaux.

Club management urged owner Jack Walker to buy Zidane and France forward Christophe Dugarry, but Walker famously replied: "Why do we need Zidane when we have Tim Sherwood?"

Sherwood had lifted the Premier League trophy a few months earlier and both Zidane and Dugarry had flown to England to talk to the club but no deal was completed.

Zidane and Dugarry went on to win the World Cup with France in 1998 and the European Championship two years later, with Zidane lifting two Italian titles with Juventus and then La Liga and the Champions League with Real Madrid.

Dugarry had spells at AC Milan, Barcelona, Marseille and back at Bordeaux, although he did end his career in England with two seasons at Birmingham City.

In 2005, just off the back of a sensational Champions League win when Liverpool fought back from 3-0 down at half-time against AC Milan before winning on penalties, Steven Gerrard upset the red half of Merseyside. He handed in a transfer request.

Chelsea boss Jose Mourinho was interested in acquiring the England midfielder's services in a potential £32m move, with Gerrard refusing to sign a new contract.

Eventually Gerrard decided to stay with Liverpool, citing "family reasons". Gerrard would go on to make more than 700 appearances for the Reds and guide them to the 2007 Champions League final, although AC Milan would get their revenge.

Ten years later, Mourinho said his failure to sign Gerrard was one of his greatest transfer disappointments.

France striker Kylian Mbappe is the record goalscorer in World Cups, helping his country win the 2018 competition and then scoring a hat-trick in the 2022 final as Les Bleus lost on penalties to Argentina.

However, he could have been a Liverpool player in 2017 as he had talks with the Reds when still at Monaco.

"I talked to Liverpool because it's the favourite club of my mum, my mum loves Liverpool," said Mbappe.

Then-Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp recently revealed how the club laid on a private jet and food for Mbappe and his family.

However, despite his mother's favourite club being the Reds, Mbappe joined Paris St-Germain, where he won six successive Ligue 1 titles before joining Real Madrid in 2024.

France striker Antoine Griezmann has had a great career, but never played in the Premier League.

But he nearly did, with Fulham making an unlikely £12m bid for him in January 2014 when the Cottagers were fighting to stay in the Premier League.

Fulham enquired about Griezmann to his club Real Sociedad and were quoted a price of £12m. In the end, the west London side spent that figure on Olympiakos striker Kostas Mitroglou, who only played three Premier League matches, scoring no goals, before the Cottagers were relegated.

Mitroglou then had loan spells back at Olympiakos and then Benfica, who he joined permanently in 2016-17.

Griezmann stayed in Spain with nine seasons over two spells at Atletico Madrid and two years at Barcelona. He helped France win the World Cup in 2018.

title: From Love Island to Commonwealth gold for McConnell
description: Team Northern Ireland boxer Jon McConnell tells BBC Sport NI of his decision to reject Love Island to pursue his childhood dream of winning Commonwealth gold, which he achieved with a split decision win over Wales' Orlando Holley-Sotomi.
fullText:
A summer spent in the sun on the Spanish island of Mallorca finding love or one spent in gloomy Glasgow getting beat up time after time?

In this unique predicament many would, without hesitation, opt for the former, but Team Northern Ireland boxer Jon McConnell went for the second option.

The 23-year-old turned down the chance to appear on the latest series of Love Island after applying and instead opted to go to the Commonwealth Games.

That decision will have felt vindicated when his hand was raised as the winner of Commonwealth gold in the men's 70kg final via split decision over Wales' Orlando Holley-Sotomi on Saturday.

He's not ruling out a future appearance in the famous villa, although that is put on hold for now as he continues to go from strength to strength in his fledgling boxing career.

"The decision [not to go on Love Island] paid off. If I had have got put out in the first round I might have went 'did I make the right decision?'," he told BBC Sport NI.

"But a gold medal now so they can give me a shout if they want."

Walsh and Rock take silver after final defeats

Boxers choose Commonwealths over Love Island chance

How close he ever really came to appearing on the reality show is a bit of mystery.

He shared a photo on his Instagram story on the morning of Saturday's final showing that on 28 December last year he had marked Saturday, 1 August 2026 as the day he would win Commonwealth gold.

That prediction came true and in impressive fashion.

Holley-Sotomi, who had been "dynamite" on his way to the final according to McConnell, had started well in the gold medal bout, but the NI fighter was unperturbed after a difficult first round.

He changed tact and opted to come roaring back, landing with some big shots of his own.

It culminated in a split decision victory and the fulfilment of a childhood dream.

"I had written that down on 28 December, but that has been a goal since I was eight or nine years of age. I didn't just write it down, I worked for it every day to get to this point and I'm here, Commonwealth Games gold medallist, it's unbelievable," he explained.

"That was a hard, hard fight. He was big, he was strong and he had knocked a few out, but I boxed well. He caught me in the first round and it stung me a bit, woke me up and we changed the tactics, I was busier and stayed away from his backhand.

"It was a close fight, it could have went either way, but I felt I landed the cleaner shots and with a bit of luck, I got there in the end."

The victory brings NI's one and only boxing gold and only their second gold of the Games overall after Kate O'Connor won the heptathlon on Wednesday.

McConnell joked that it was "not bad company" to be in and how he is determined to, like O'Connor, keep striving for further success.

"I was waiting for the right tournament that would put me on the world stage. I was building and building, so it's time to push on for bigger things and we'll see what happens next."

McConnell may have taken the only gold but it was a successful Games for the boxing team as a whole with half of the 12-strong squad taking home a medal.

Michaela Walsh and Kaci Rock also leave Glasgow with a silver while Willie John McCartan, Garyn McAllister and Jude Gallagher, champion four years ago, all claimed bronze.

There was much made of the age profiles of the squad heading over to Glasgow, with eight aged 25 or under and nine competing at their first Games.

While Louis Rooney, Janssen Hill, Eoghan Quinn and JP Hale all fell at the first hurdle, they were the only four to not win at least one bout.

Nicole Clyde and Caitlin Fryers made it to the quarter-final stage while McCartan, McAllister and Gallagher exited at the semi-finals.

Some did receive the luck of the draw, with Walsh, Rock, Walsh, Hill, McAllister and McCartan going straight through to quarter-finals where they were one win away from a medal, but they still had to seize the initiative and push on.

For Walsh, it was a fourth successive medal at the Games, her third silver to add to the two from 2014 and 2018 and the gold from 2022.

She joins bowler Neil Booth, shooter Martin Millar plus Mike Bull and Lady Mary Peters from athletics on four medals at the Games.

Only shooter David Calvert has won more with eight.

She was "speechless" to hear her name mentioned among those greats, but her achievements demonstrate her longevity and she's not finished yet.

"I'm proud of my performances throughout the whole tournament. I have Europeans now in six weeks and I'm using this as a springboard to that and I'm ready to go again," she said.

"[Four medals] It's obviously an amazing achievement. I'm lucky, I love boxing and I'm doing what I love. It's a lifetime of work and it's amazing for the medals to show that."

While Walsh is used to such an occasion, it was easy for younger members of the team to be overawed at a first multi-sport competition, but Rock showed maturity beyond her years, particularly in fighting back to win the semi-final after losing the first round.

For Rock, like McConnell, it's a first major medal at her first Games and she believes it is just the start for her and many of her team-mates.

"I think so many people doubted our team because we're a younger, fresher and inexperienced team but we have six medals coming home.

"We've proven we're only getting started and there's so much more to come."

title: The four dramatic days that shook Infantino and world football
description: BBC Sport's Simon Stone reflects on the unravelling of Gianni Infantino's plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions.
fullText:
Any hope Gianni Infantino might have had of tiptoeing away from the scene of his World Cup private-investment wreckage having sustained only minor damage to his reputation disappeared on Saturday.

Uefa - the governing body of European football - went straight for the head of world game, saying it had "lost confidence" in his leadership.

It was one of the most ferocious statements ever aimed at the holder of that position.

Words such as "shabby" and "secret schemes" spoke for themselves.

It came after a dramatic four days for football that sparked memories of the European Super League debacle of 2021.

The ESL was a splinter league formed by 12 of Europe's biggest clubs, including six from the Premier League.

Former England defender Gary Neville echoed the thoughts of many when he referred to it as "pure greed". It quickly unravelled.

Infantino's private-investment plan did not have a catchy title, and lasted two days longer than the ESL.

But despite football's world governing body confirming the proposal was being withdrawn on Saturday, the infamy will linger much longer.

At the top level, football is a vast, money-making enterprise. The sums players and executives earn is beyond the scope of 'ordinary' fans.

But have we discovered there is a line that cannot be crossed?

Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Infantino's Fifa leadership

Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan

Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?

The question many have asked around Infantino's plan is tied into a separate - but critical - aspect of the fundamental reasons behind this week unravelling.

Fifa is a not-for-profit organisation. It has huge financial reserves - over $2bn (£1.48bn) - and is expected to announce record revenues of about $15bn (£11.13bn) in relation to this summer's World Cup.

Given that backdrop - and the reality some countries simply did not need the extra $40m (£29.67m) being offered for football development initiatives if they signed up to Infantino's plan by 19 September - many wondered why private investment was needed in the first place.

It was a question that needed to be asked. But that did not happen in public - or, it has become apparent, privately in Fifa's corridors of power.

Many of Fifa's most senior people - from vice-presidents to special advisers and executives - did not have a chance to ask any questions, simply because they had no clue the plans were being drawn up.

Uefa had strongly opposed the plans from the moment they became public. When they were dropped, its response was damning.

"The current Fifa leadership has not only lost Uefa's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family," it said in a statement.

"When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of Fifa's member associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said: 'Of course we have to be transparent.'

"He told the assembled stakeholders: 'The money of Fifa is your money. It's not the money of the Fifa president. You are the national associations and the money of Fifa has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.'

"On both these promises, he has failed to deliver."

It was not the first time a lack of transparency had been highlighted.

Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa - president of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), and one of eight Fifa vice-presidents - referred to it too.

He said any future plans that may impact global football should be presented to members "in a timely, transparent and meaningful manner".

"The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game," he added.

Football Australia chair Anter Isaac said trust was earned "not simply through good decisions, but through the integrity of the processes that lead to them".

"Football has never stood still, nor should it," he said.

"Some principles, however, should never change. Integrity. Independence. Good governance. Transparency. Meaningful consultation. Due process. These are not constraints on progress."

With the ESL, it was the fans that drew the line - backed by the Premier League, the Football Association and even Prince William.

The plan in 2021 was for the clubs who took part to remain in their national leagues, but also to play each other in a new midweek European competition, which would have rivalled the Champions League.

Critics argued it was a way for the clubs to enrich themselves in a closed league that would have increased commercial and broadcasting income, and the principle of a domestic football pyramid should be protected.

After 72 hours of criticism, the plans all but fell apart. In the aftermath, it was claimed clubs did not get the opportunity to present a rounded case because the outline plan was leaked to the media. That meant the reaction was so fierce any counter-argument would have been lost.

This week has been remarkably similar - except this time, it was people in football who drew the line in the sand.

The only real difference is Fifa did put its counterargument forward in the early hours of Friday - along with an assertion its "planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports".

As with the ESL, by that point the direction of travel was already established and could not be changed.

With sentiment so strongly against the plans, a damning statement from Fifa's respected chief operating officer Kevin Lamour would have been a crushing blow.

He described the controversial plans as "the project of one person" and claimed Fifa's administration had been "deceived". BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.

Lamour acknowledged he had a duty of loyalty to his employer but also to "certain values" and supporting his colleagues.

"Our mission - the mission of the hundreds of passionate, dedicated, and exemplary Fifa employees - is to serve football," he wrote.

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it. I will understand and respect that decision.

"At least I'll sleep well tonight."

Infantino has developed a close relationship with US President Donald Trump, and the pair helped present the World Cup to Spain less than a fortnight ago.

If Infantino was looking for assistance from Trump when he was asked about the proposals for the first time on Friday, he did not get it. Trump said he had not spoken to the 56-year-old about the plans.

A report in the New York Post, which broke the story of the plans being withdrawn, quoted an unnamed source saying the situation had become a "brand nightmare" for Joshua Kushner - brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared.

Kusher founded Thrive Eternal - the American venture capital firm that would have led the proposed investor group had Fifa's plans gone ahead.

As with the ESL, in the end, Infantino was left with no choice but to withdraw the idea.

Now he is left to clear up the mess and build bridges, amid claims support for his re-election as Fifa president in March is receding.

Speaking before Uefa's statement on Saturday, its vice-president Laura McAllister spoke to BBC Radio Four's Today programme.

"All of the confederations will be considering options now," she said.

"There will be moves, I'm sure, to encourage people to stand, but it's early days yet.

"The key thing this week has been to defeat this proposal with unity and consensus and that's what we've been able to do."

Once again, football has shown that while it is prepared to accept many things - and not all of them will be popular - there are some lines that cannot be crossed.

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

title: Dog walk and expletive text - key findings in Vondrousova anti-doping case
description: The full report into 2023 Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova's four-year ban for refusing a doping test has been released - BBC Sport analyses the key findings.
fullText:
Recent Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova receiving a four-year ban for refusing to take a doping test was a punishment which sent shockwaves through tennis.

The Czech, who became the first unseeded player to win the Wimbledon women's singles title in 2023, would not let a doping control officer into her Prague home to conduct the test in December 2025.

In June, it was announced the 27-year-old would be suspended for four years - the starting point for any player who refuses or evades a test.

On Friday, the independent tribunal which imposed the punishment released its full written report about the case - which it described as a "very unfortunate matter" but which offered "no compelling justification" for a shorter ban.

From how walking her dog undermined her case, to the lack of understanding players seem to have about doping rules, BBC Sport analyses some of the key findings.

Vondrousova, who also reached the French Open final in 2019 and won the Tokyo 2020 Olympics silver medal, claimed she feared for her safety when the doping officer arrived at her flat at 8pm on 3 December.

She was alone in her apartment and told the officer via the intercom that she would not open the door.

The tribunal's report said Vondrousova called her agent to ask about doping protocol, and sent a text message to her boyfriend which said someone from doping control had arrived - using an expletive to describe them.

There is some dispute about what happened next, with the doping officer saying the pair had two exchanges over the intercom, but Vondrousova saying there was only one.

Both sides agree they met face-to-face about 10 minutes later when Vondrousova went outside to walk her Italian Greyhound dog.

That is when Vondrousova reiterated she would not take the test and signed a form which acknowledged her stance.

The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) - the body tasked with overseeing a clean and fair sport - said it had little option other than to seek a four-year suspension.

The tribunal agreed with the ITIA. It ruled she had provided "no compelling justification" for refusing a test.

On Friday, the tribunal said: "This is a very unfortunate manner in which the player made a decision in the heat of the moment to refuse doping control, in a state of stress and anxiety, with significant consequences."

Ex-Wimbledon champion Vondrousova given four-year ban

One of the key parts of Vondrousova's mitigation centred around her safety concerns.

The former world number six said she felt scared when the officer approached her door "late at night" without, she claimed, properly identifying themselves or following protocol.

Vondrousova cited the horrific knife attack on her fellow Czech player Petra Kvitova - who was stabbed by an intruder at her home in 2016 - as a reason why she did not open the door.

However, the ITIA contested Vondorousova's case that she felt her safety was at risk, and the reasons why they said they disagreed included:

the area of Prague where she lives is "relatively crime-free"

the comparison with Kvitova's attack was an "exaggeration"

walking her dog was "entirely inconsistent with identifying a potential threat"

The ITIA also noted Vondrousova did not raise any concerns about her safety in the exchanges with her agent and her boyfriend.

In her defence to the tribunal, Vondrousova said another reason why she did not want to open the door was because she suffered from acute stress reaction and an anxiety disorder.

The tribunal acknowledged the situation would have led to anxiety, but said her wider arguments about safety and stress were not "exceptional circumstances".

Vondrousova's case has been another example of how some players have revealed they do not know the doping rules.

After the incident in December, Vondrousova posted an Instagram story in which she accused the officer of not following rules because the call was outside her one-hour whereabouts slot.

The whereabouts rule means players must give a time and location for an hour where they can be tested every day of the year. They are also able to be tested outside this 60-minute slot.

"Unpredictable testing is an essential tool to protect clean sport," ITIA chief executive Karen Moorhouse said in June.

"The tribunal ultimately supported that principle. This case is an important reminder that players can be tested at any time, in any place, and that refusal comes with significant risk."

The tribunal's report noted how Vondrousova said she did not know she could be tested outside the one-hour slot, and claimed she had never been tested at home outside this window before.

She also said her agent did not know out-of-hours testing was possible.

The ITIA argued that "any lack of understanding" of the anti-doping rules by an experienced player like Vondrousova - who has taken 83 tests since 2018 - was "not credible".

Is tennis catching doping cheats or ruining careers?

Vondrousova plans to appeal against the decision and will lodge her case with the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) before the 11 August deadline, BBC Sport has been told.

She has not played since January as she dealt with the case, having already dropped to 122nd in the world when her ban was announced in June.

If her appeal is unsuccessful, she will not be able to play again until June 2030.

That means she will be almost 31 years old when free to return - if she wishes.

Whatever happens with the appeal process, Vondrousova's refusal to take the test has already cost her a considerable chunk of what should be the peak years of an impressive career.

It also acts as a serious warning to other players that missing a test will not be tolerated - a deterrent intended by the ITIA, who mission statement is providing 'tennis you can trust'.

title: 'It is good to dream' - Aina eyes Champions League spot under Glasner
description: Nottingham Forest's Ola Aina says he has "dusted off the cobwebs" for wing-back favouring head coach Oliver Glasner and believes that the club can "dream big" again this season.  "It has been hard work but it has been good," Aina told BBC East Midlands' Charlie Slater when asked about life under Glasner.
fullText:
Nottingham Forest's Ola Aina says he has "dusted off the cobwebs" for wing-back favouring head coach Oliver Glasner and believes that the club can "dream big" again this season.

The 29-year-old right-back is looking forward to "cracking on" with the season after a hamstring tear, sustained in September 2025, hampered his playing time in 2025-26.

"It has been hard work but it has been good," Aina told BBC East Midlands' Charlie Slater when asked about life under Glasner. "Everyone is buying into his ideas and his philosophy. It is really exciting for all of us boys.

"He is a winner. He has shown what he can do over the past few seasons with Crystal Palace, with the right backing and with time, so hopefully he can do that here as well.

"We have to dream big - why can't we? We have everything that a team needs to be successful, so it is down to us to hit the ground running, put the hard work in, stay together and be locked in.

"Why not push for a Champions League finish? It is good to dream."

On Glasner's playing style heavily relying on wing-backs, the full-back replied: "I used to play as a wing-back in Italy, so it has been a few years!

"I told him to give me a few weeks to just dust off the cobwebs and get the engines going again.

"As a full-back, you can pick and choose the right times to go. As a wing-back, you have to go every time because you need to be that support in attack but also get back to help your centre-backs at times. It is a balance.

"I'm wishing for more goals in my game. I hope I get some little tap-ins here and there this season. I don't mind how many - a goal is a goal. I haven't got a celebration picked out just yet, but I'm sure I can think of one."

title: 'His football is very intensity-based, but he shows a lot of flexibility'
description: German football journalist Constantin Eckner says he rates Matthias Jaissle, who is expected to replace Eddie Howe at Newcastle, "very highly".  Jaissle joined Al-Ahli in 2023 and led the Saudi club to back-to-back AFC Champions League titles in 2024-25 and 2025-26.  "He might be the right man for the job," said Eckner on BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast.
fullText:
German football journalist Constantin Eckner says he rates Matthias Jaissle, who is expected to replace Eddie Howe at Newcastle, "very highly".

Jaissle joined Al-Ahli in 2023 and led the Saudi club to back-to-back AFC Champions League titles in 2024-25 and 2025-26.

"He might be the right man for the job," said Eckner on BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast. "There are a couple of uncertainties regarding Newcastle's transfers this summer, so we don't know how the team will look when the Premier League starts or once deadline day has passed.

"But I rate Matthias Jaissle very highly. His football is still very intensity-based, but he shows a lot of flexibility.

"Jaissle, like Fabian Hurzeler at Brighton, is a young coach who is very good at coaching intensity to all kind of players.

"One big advantage I have been told about him is that he communicates very efficiently and precisely. He doesn't ramble - it's clear-cut and his English has improved massively.

"We have to see how he deals with the pressure, but he is smart and able to put things into perspective by himself."

Listen to the full episode of Football Daily on BBC Sounds

title: Scottish Premiership is back on Friday - here's why you shouldn't miss it
description: BBC Scotland takes a look at the top talking points going into the new Scottish Premiership season.
fullText:
It seems like it was only yesterday traffic cones across Boston were being turned into street art and Billy Gilmour had transformed into a Major League Baseball pitcher.

The star-spangled pizazz has only just subsided after the crashing wave of World Cup disappointment for Scotland, but now we're back to the real stuff.

The Scottish Premiership, surely the globe's top league for compulsive viewing, returns this Friday.

Here's the top takes to hook you back in.

What is the magic number to win Scottish Premiership?

Who has your Premiership club brought in & let go this summer?

Hearts' players were on the brink of history and immortality. It was nine minutes away.

Four decades of Old Firm dominance was that close to toppling. The season-long league leaders were drawing with holders Celtic in Glasgow as the game crept into the 87th minute.

It looked like they were just about to hold until Daizen Maeda struck to trigger bedlam in Paradise.

Ugly scenes followed Celtic's third deep into injury time as Hearts headed straight for the team bus, eventually reemerging outside Tynecastle with tears spilling from their faces.

Since then, the backbone of that team has been deconstructed. Boss Derek McInnes has departed for Tynecastle, taking with him captain and talisman Lawrence Shankland, as well as midfield controller Cammy Devlin.

Wouter Vrancken has arrived from Sint-Truiden and the Belgian has suffered a tumultuous start.

A 6-0 hiding from Sturm Graz sent Hearts tumbling out of Champions League qualifying, with the Tynecastle support looking at the club's analytical approach to signings to somehow hoist them back to the lofty heights they hit last term.

"Hearts just look as if it's just a new squad flung in together, with the manager too, trying to find their way," said former striker Ryan Stevenson.

"You don't get time in football, it's game after game after game.

"If you don't get results, we all know what Tynecastle is like. It can be electric, but can they deal with the stadium turning? Are they big enough characters to deal with that?

"If they don't play well, I would give it to mid-September, and it would not be nice."

Are there already worrying signs for Vrancken's Hearts?

The short answer is... well... we don't really know yet.

Last season's domestic double was followed by Martin O'Neill remaining as boss, offering some continuity after the most unique of campaigns.

However, there still has been plenty of disquiet among supporters.

Anti-board sentiment was present last term before and after Brendan Rodgers' shock departure, with Wilfried Nancy's alarmingly short tenure doing little to help.

In a bid to quell matters, a fan engagement programme, external was launched on Thursday.

At the heart of the unrest though, ultimately, is what - and who - happens on the park.

The Parkhead side have made two signings this summer - Camilo Duran and Kasper Hogh - for reported combined fees of around £15m.

However, talismanic forward Daizen Maeda has left to join Ipswich Town and O'Neill is keen to get high-calibre players through the door sooner rather than later.

Celtic have been linked extensively with Real Oviedo and Egypt winger Haissem Hassan, as well as Paderborn midfielder Mika Baur.

"I think we're trying to get some quality into the football club," O'Neill told Sky Sports.

Celtic 'a really good match' for record signing Hogh

The former Ibrox player was so close to legendary status and a league winner's medal with Hearts in May. Now, he's aiming to do just that in Glasgow.

A 2-1 win over St Etienne and a goalless draw with West Ham in pre-season friendlies have offered tentative encouragement. Ultimately, Rangers need consistency and an identity that was lacking last term.

Danny Rohl hauled Rangers in the title hunt going into the split, only to then lose four of their five remaining matches.

Long-term captain James Tavernier has left, so too have goalkeeper Jack Butland and forward Oliver Antman.

McInnes and Rangers appear to have made some shrewd moves in the transfer market already in the opposite direction.

South Africa defender Olwethu Makhanya is the eighth new recruit to arrive, while Shankland has been appointed skipper and the acquisition of young Serbia international midfielder Vanja Dragojevic looks a savvy one.

But is it enough to shift the balance of power away from Glasgow's east end?

Is McInnes era giving Rangers fans fewer fears of failure?

Scotland is not alone with an obsession over video assistant referees and the application of the technology across the game.

Earlier this week associations were told VAR should only intervene over "blatant" incidents.

Incredibly, this will be the fifth season of VAR's use in Scotland and fans still remain divided.

In the most high-profile incident, former Motherwell midfielder Elliot Watt and McInnes were both sanctioned for fuming over the decision to award Celtic a late penalty at Fir Park in the penultimate game of last season.

Watt described it as "the worst VAR decision in history", while McInnes claimed it was "disgusting".

Last week St Johnstone manager Simo Valakari said he believes the system will get better after a meeting with the Scottish Football Association's VAR manager Martin Atkinson.

The Finn also said maybe in Scotland there needs to be more "patience".

As if all that wasn't enough...

We have five managers starting permanent tenures at clubs in McInnes, Vrancken, Alfred Johansson at Motherwell and O'Neill and Craig McLeish taking on the role proper at Celtic and St Mirren respectively.

Speaking of Motherwell, Scotland's answer to Barcelona last season have lost key players in Watt and New Zealand World Cup hero Elijah Just, but have managed to retain their methodical footballing approach as well as the likes of Tawanda Maswanhise and Lukas Fadinger.

Can Johansson kick on from the Jens Berthel Askou blueprint and keep the crowds swelling at Fir Park?

You also have a first full season at Pittodrie for Stephen Robinson and proper grass at Kilmarnock, who have ditched their artificial surface.

As always, the BBC has you covered.

Online, you can 

We will also provide live text coverage of every single Scottish Premiership match.

You can follow the latest video content across all our social channels, as well as on the BBC Scottish Football YouTube channel for bespoke video.

On television, Sportscene has you covered for highlights starting on Friday as Dundee United host Rangers. You can catch the show on BBC iPlayer and BBC One Scotland at 23:35 BST.

And on radio, follow exclusive radio commentary and top punditry on Sportsound, while Stuart Cosgrove and Tam Cowan, the Odd Couple of Scottish Football, will continue to bring you the best petty and ill-informed show on the airwaves, Off The Ball.

title: 'Change is inevitable' - Liverpool CEO on FSG, Iraola and consortium talks
description: Liverpool Billy Hogan talks to BBC Sport in New York about investment, transition and why FSG aren't done yet.
fullText:
With Liverpool stating that they have more than 26 million supporters in the USA, there is little surprise over why the Reds chose America as the destination for their pre-season tour.

This has been quite the summer for football here and Billy Hogan, CEO of Liverpool and Fenway Sports Group (FSG), insists the aim is to build on that after what has been a "super difficult year" for the club "for lots of different reasons."

Hogan is speaking to BBC Sport in New York ahead of Andoni Iraola's side taking on Wrexham at the famous Yankee Stadium on Wednesday evening at 19:30 local time, 00:30 BST.

However, for all the excitement around a new era on the pitch, it is events off the pitch that must be addressed first.

Last week, FSG, which owns Liverpool, confirmed that a consortium led by Amit Bhatia, a British-Indian millionaire businessman, was in talks over a strategic minority investment in the club. Those talks have been ongoing and there is a growing belief that a deal will be done.

"Look, John Henry (the principal owner) and FSG have always said that if there was an interest in an investment that would help the football club, then they would consider it. That was said many years ago and that remains the case here," Hogan tells BBC Sport.

"At this point, I wouldn't say anything different to the statement that a consortium led, managed and represented by Amit Bhatia has come forward and expressed an interest in a minority investment."

Hogan, who has been with FSG since they purchased Liverpool for £300m in 2010, does stress though that they are still very much committed to the project and that news of this development should not be seen as a sign of the company, which also owns the Major League Baseball franchise, Boston Red Sox, stepping away.

According to the Financial Times, a deal with the consortium led by Bhatia would value Liverpool at more than £4.5bn.

"There's a huge opportunity still," Hogan says. "This is the biggest and most popular sport in the world and we're one of the biggest clubs in the biggest league in the biggest sport in the world. So that's a great place for us to be. The Premier League has a tremendous amount of momentum behind it.

"We've definitely not peaked. We're in a good place to continue to grow and that's why everyone across both sides of the club, football and business and whether they kick a ball or not, is focused on driving the club forward and winning trophies.

"On the pitch, our goal every season is to win trophies. Off the pitch, our priority is to continue driving overall revenues and expand and build the club.

"We're really happy with the trajectory and direction of the club - we were fifth in the Deloitte Football Money League and had the highest revenue (£702m) in the Premier League.

"All of that investment, as has always been the case since 2010, goes back into the club. It's about running the club sustainably."

Who is potential investor Bhatia?

Consortium in talks to buy Liverpool minority stake

After a record summer spend last season of £450m, Liverpool were disappointing on the pitch.

Ultimately, that led to the sacking of Arne Slot at the end of the campaign. Senior players like Mohamed Salah, Andy Robertson and Ibrahima Konate all left on free transfers too.

It has been a summer of change at Liverpool with Michael Edwards stepping down as FSG's CEO of football, primarily because plans of multi-club ownership were abandoned.

Meanwhile, Richard Hughes, Liverpool's sporting director, is linked with a move to Al Hilal in Saudi Arabia. There is certainly a question of stability.

"Transition and change is inevitable in football. In our case, with a new coach coming in, there's real excitement around Andoni's mindset and philosophy that supporters will really enjoy," says Hogan.

"That will take time but in terms of transition, I would send a message that we are in a very healthy place as a football club - the leadership from ownership is in a very steady place and we're looking forward to the next season and the season ahead."

Hogan insists that regardless of the personnel changes, the club model remains the same and they will continue to stick to their principles.

"It's important to keep in mind that last season, a considerable amount was invested but also generated in terms of sales of players going out," he says. "Over the course of FSG's stewardship, the investment has always been focused on doing what's best to put us in a place to win.

"Sometimes that means significant expense and other times it doesn't like in the summer of 2024 when there was only one addition (Federico Chiesa for £12.5m). It depends on where we are at the club and the improvements needed. Ultimately Mike Gordon, who is really our managing owner, will make those decisions."

There is an increased focus on the women's team too, who finished 11th in the WSL last season and haven't won the top-flight title since 2014.

"To be self-critical, that is probably an area that we maybe took our eye off the ball several years ago but we've changed that," says Hogan.

"We now have one of the best training centres at AXA Melwood, we are investing in the squad and we will approach the women's team the same way we approach the men's team - which is to run it sustainably. There's tremendous growth in the women's game and a huge opportunity going forward to really drive that."

Liverpool preparing opening bid for PSG's Barcola

It is still remarkable to think now that the club was on the verge of administration when FSG took over in 2010.

It hasn't all been plain sailing. As recently as this year, Hogan wrote to fans over ticket price increases. The club cut the size of their planned rise in ticket prices for the next couple of seasons after fan protests.

However, under FSG's stewardship, Anfield has been transformed, with two of the four stands developed in the last decade.

"Back when FSG acquired LFC, a number of similarities were drawn with Boston Red Sox and Liverpool and one of them was this idea of an iconic venue that truly sits in the community," says Hogan. "One of the things we're focused on now is making improvements in the footprint around Anfield the neighbourhood whether that's infrastructure or transport and getting people in on non-match days. We're proud of how we've expanded while keeping the soul but also modernising it in the way that's befitting of the football club.

"Football doesn't give you much time to sit back and reflect. What I would say I am most proud of is that the club is in such a positive and good financial position. If you go back to that point in 2010, the club was literally on the brink of bankruptcy. Now it has the right foundations underneath it. There's improvements across the infrastructure, the ability to stay at Anfield for the long-term and the stuff that doesn't always get headlines but are super important for the health of the club.

"Ultimately, it's about winning trophies and I wish we could win more but we've been fortunate to win a few.

"I think our supporters have had a great time and I often think about the fan parks at the Champions League finals - we lost a couple but just that joy and the memories and frankly the fun of it is what I look back from time to time. And it's something that everyone associated with Liverpool should be proud of because it happens together and we all want this club to be the best in the world."

After a torrid year for Liverpool, where better to start looking ahead than in New York, the city of dreams?

title: Is World Cup sell-off plan a step too far by Infantino?
description: BBC Sport explores why Fifa president Gianni Infantino feels powerful enough to sell off stakes in the World Cup - and what the consequences could be.
fullText:
Gianni Infantino is billing it as the democratisation of football.

But Fifa's announcement that it aims to sell off stakes in its football competitions - including the World Cup - to private investors via associates of US President Donald Trump has been met with incredulity and rage from fans, politicians and regional governing bodies.

The big selling point, according to Infantino, is $40m (£30m) in funding given to all Fifa countries to "develop the game" once the deal is finalised.

The Swiss has set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his plans if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m).

This is the boldest move Infantino, an administrator who views himself as a world leader on par with presidents and prime ministers, has made in the decade since he became Fifa president.

If Fifa pushes the plan through, he will have consolidated his power for the long-term future and made investors wealthy along the way.

So why exactly does Infantino feel powerful enough to enact something so controversial, and what could the consequences be?

Infantino has enough support to suggest the plan is more likely to go ahead than not.

Since being elected Fifa president in 2016, Infantino has earned long-standing, widespread backing from many countries in Africa, Asia, and the Americas, which have gained financially from various policies he has managed.

They include the expansion of the World Cup to 48 teams, the growth in commercial and broadcast revenue Fifa has overseen, and a programme which allocates millions in funding directly to member countries every year.

That gives him a base of support which constitutes more than half of Fifa's 211 members.

Fifa votes require a simple majority - if more than half vote in favour, Infantino's plan will come into effect.

The proposal will appeal to many nations, particularly those lower down the football food chain, for whom a £15m windfall would be more than they would ordinarily make over several years.

The level of backing Infantino enjoys appears to have emboldened his approach to the presidency. Decisions such as the introduction of hydration breaks and a musical half-time show to the World Cup were taken by his administration without a vote of members, and would have been deemed unthinkable when he took charge a decade ago.

And his close relationship with Trump is key too.

The investment fund Fifa is dealing with - Thrive Capital - is led by Josh Kushner, the brother-in-law of Trump's daughter Ivanka.

Fifa says Greg Maffei, the American former president of Formula 1 owner Liberty Media who has donated to Trump's political campaigns in the past, is acting as a "key commercial advisor".

The proposal follows years of Infantino making overt attempts to deepen his and Fifa's ties with Trump.

He created a Peace Prize and awarded it to Trump. He opened a Fifa office in Trump Tower, New York. He allowed the Club World Cup trophy to be kept in the Oval Office at the White House. He laughed along during Trump's inauguration speech in which he threatened World Cup co-hosts Canada and Mexico.

And last week, Infantino heavily mimicked Trump's language when he released a statement describing those who criticised aspects of the organisation of the World Cup as "so consumed by hate and criticism".

Working with Trump associates on the plan allows Infantino to harness the power of the bond he has cultivated with the world's most powerful person, with the promise of a mutually beneficial outcome.

Fifa has engaged in discussions about the potential sell-off unilaterally, generating anger among nations and regions who feel it was done behind their backs.

But while there is a significant element of risk attached to this move, the chances of Infantino being brought down by it are slim, given how strong support is for him elsewhere.

Fifa would receive a huge influx of cash in one go if the plan is approved, and the proportion earmarked for national federations would be made available from 1 January 2027, according to a letter sent to each country by Infantino.

He added: "The decision whether or not to proceed with this proposal belongs entirely to you.

"In exchange, all that is required is your trust - everything else remains the same."

The appeal is clear - vote to help make us richer and we'll make you richer too.

But each World Cup makes significantly more money than the last - it will probably be worth far 

If Fifa sells stakes now, then the private investors will share in the rewards of that growth in the coming years, rather than Fifa and football doing so alone.

And ultimately, Fifa is a non-profit organisation under Swiss law, meaning its ultimate goal is - theoretically, at least - the long-term wellbeing of football rather than making a profit.

The big winners from the plan, then, would arguably be some of the smaller football nations, the private investors, and Infantino.

"What we know so far about how some national federations spend their money raises a lot of doubts about whether the money reaches the levels of football which Fifa promises," says Miguel Maduro, a former chairman of Fifa's governance committee.

Maduro claims he quit that role after 10 months because Infantino and Fifa's wider leadership disagreed with how the committee was operating.

"Fifa works as a political cartel - it is fed and supported on a system of patronage, that works through the money Fifa distributes to national federations. There have been cases of corruption," he added.

"There is a very high likelihood that this [proposal] will be approved.

"It is a form of legalised bribe."

BBC Sport has contacted Fifa for comment about Maduro's assessment.

Private equity investment has already transformed sports in the USA.

Rules have been changed in baseball, basketball, American football and ice hockey to allow for more minority investments in the past decade, causing team values to skyrocket.

And La Liga and Ligue 1 have already sold portions of their operations to private equity firm CVC Capital Partners in exchange for an immediate influx of money.

Infantino is hopping on a trend in sports economics rather than trying out something entirely new, but stands to further entrench his own power if he succeeds.

Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan

Uefa and PM criticise Infantino World Cup plan

Infantino's proposal has deepened his ongoing conflict with European governing body Uefa - the most powerful and wealthy regional organiser.

Uefa President Aleksander Ceferin boycotted the World Cup final in protest against Fifa's decision to overturn USA striker Folarin Balogun's suspension after an intervention from Trump.

That followed a series of Uefa announcements making clear it would not follow Fifa policy on controversial issues including dynamic ticket pricing and hydration breaks.

One of the cornerstones of the division between the two is that Fifa's revamped and expanded Club World Cup has become a clear, direct threat to Uefa's Champions League.

Previously Uefa was the only organisation which ran an international club football competition featuring the best players, watched by billions around the world and generating significant profits.

Last summer Fifa muscled in on that elite club football territory, adding teams from other continents to the mix.

Some national federations have expressed anger that they found out about the plans only when Fifa made them public, but crucially, many of the statements released so far have not explicitly condemned the concept of the sell-off itself.

That said, BBC Sport understands many Uefa members are angry about the plan and that a meeting is set to be convened for them to discuss a response.

On Tuesday Uefa said Fifa's plan is "to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends".

Some reports indicate a threat by European nations to boycott the World Cup could be possible. The theory is that a World Cup without European countries would severely compromise the tournament's value to Fifa.

But the chances of that coming to pass are debatable.

Europe is one of the main hosts of the next tournament in 2030, with Spain and Portugal holding the majority of matches alongside Morocco, and Spain is currently lobbying hard to win the right to host the final ahead of Morocco.

There is also a women's World Cup next year in Brazil, which could be an early target for any action, if Uefa does want to take a bold step of its own.

Uefa could potentially find and field a candidate to stand against Infantino in next year's presidential election, but given Uefa nations comprise only 55 votes, they would be unlikely to win.

If Ceferin and other European leaders really want to fight Infantino's plan as hard as possible, they must be willing to make a big move of some sort very quickly indeed.

For now, Infantino is as emboldened as he has ever been.

title: Have season ticket holders 'passed their sell-by date' for clubs?
description: BBC Radio Manchester's Gaz Drinkwater and Joe McGrath discussed restrictions on season tickets in the latest episode of The Devils' Advocate.  Manchester United has restricted the accounts of "thousands" of fans, in an operation aimed at identifying potential ticket touts.  Drinkwater said he has "full sympathy" for fans who have fallen under the restrictions despite not being involved as touts.
fullText:
BBC Radio Manchester's Gaz Drinkwater and Joe McGrath discussed restrictions on season tickets in the latest episode of The Devils' Advocate.

Manchester United has restricted the accounts of "thousands" of fans, in an operation aimed at identifying potential ticket touts.

Drinkwater said he has "full sympathy" for fans who have fallen under the restrictions despite not being involved as touts.

"It's pretty obvious that these were fans that were not touting tickets," Drinkwater said.

"I love that Manchester United fans have made such a massive, loud deal about this and football fans have got behind it as well because hopefully that means that these appeals will be listened to."

Football finance expert Kieran Maguire joined the podcast and gave his thoughts on why United might be taking this course of action.

Maguire said: "There's the theoretical one which is perfectly understandable. There's an awful lot of touting at Manchester United as with other big clubs - Liverpool are similar, Arsenal are similar, Chelsea and so on. There's a lot of people making a lot of money through the resale of tickets.

"The other issue is that season ticket holders, to a certain extent, have passed their sell-by date as far as the senior people at the club are concerned. If you're a local Red and you're going 19 times a season to Old Trafford, you're not going to the merchandise 19 times a season.

"You're paying high but not excessive prices for your ticket and those tickets could be repackaged by the club and they could send you to a warehouse in Trafford Park and give you a pie and a pint before the match and get a former player to tell a few anecdotes and they could sell those tickets for £200-£300 a pop. That's what the club wants."

On how the club can manage the situation without upsetting the loyal fans, Maguire said: "There's no easy way around this. Nobody is denying that touting isn't a problem at the club but the way that they have taken [to deal with it] has been quite unpleasant."
