title: How do Manchester City manage the Rodri dilemma?
description: BBC Sport looks at what City's new-look midfield could be like and whether it is time to cash in on Rodri.
fullText:
Replacing a manager after 10 years is no easy feat, let alone when there appears to be a squad overhaul too.

Four of the starters in City's Treble-winning side of 2022-23 - Manuel Akanji, Nathan Ake, Bernardo Silva and John Stones - have left this summer, with the Blues signing £116m Elliot Anderson and promising 17-year-old Jeremy Monga.

And the changes might not end there.

Fresh from captaining Spain to World Cup victory, Rodri will head for back surgery on Monday with just a year left on his contract, amid increasing speculation about his future.

It is not clear how long the 30-year-old will spend on the sidelines, but one thing new boss Enzo Maresca was clear on in his first news conference was that he wants to keep him.

But with reports that Real Madrid are "operating on the basis" of Rodri joining them,, external what do City do?

Will they look to cash in when Rodri returns to fitness, or keep to Maresca's stance?

And how might Maresca's midfield operate - with or without Rodri?

When Rodri returned from an anterior cruciate ligament injury last year, there will have been plenty who wondered whether he would return to the Ballon d'Or-winning levels he had reached at his peak.

Pep Guardiola - the man Maresca has replaced - said last October: "In the World Cup, he will be the best Rodri, and next season he will be the best Rodri."

Guardiola was proved right on the first count. Not only did Rodri captain Spain to World Cup success but he was also awarded the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player.

Maresca was unequivocal when asked for his view on Friday.

"I think every manager wants to have Rodri because he is a top player," he said.

"But now, surgery on Monday... he needs a holiday... he needs to rest and recover and then he will be back with us."

The plan seems clear, therefore - look to retain one of the best players in world football rather than sell him.

But there will have to be contingencies in place.

One of these will be the presence of Anderson, while City are monitoring 18-year-old Lille midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi, who impressed for Morocco in the World Cup.

To understand how Rodri, Anderson and someone like Bouaddi might come together, it is key to understand Maresca's game model.

As a disciple of positional play, he draws comparisons between his football and chess.

"There are a lot of similarities," Maresca said. "The most important is positional play and strategy.

"For a coach, it's important to have the mentality of a chess player: develop a plan, study counter-moves, choose the arrangement of the pieces."

Maresca's strategy has largely been rooted in an on-the-ball shape that looks like a 3-2-2-3.

One of Rodri's most useful qualities in a Maresca side would be his ability to move between these predefined positions on the pitch.

Throughout the World Cup, for example, we saw him drop into the backline when former City team-mate Aymeric Laporte pushed up with the ball.

Naturally, Rodri spent most of the game in a holding midfield position, but when space opened up he was more than capable of pushing forward too.

At their best, Maresca's sides use rotations of players within the 3-2-2-3. His innovation often comes in the form of creating this shape in new ways.

Defending as a 4-4-2 before attacking in the 3-2-2-3, it was Stones who stepped up from centre-back into a midfield pair with Rodri during City's Treble-winning season, when Maresca was assistant manager.

At Chelsea, one of Maresca's more unique tweaks involved playing Moises Caicedo at right-back. Defending with a back four before again attacking in a 3-2-2-3 shape, Caicedo would move from right-back into one of the holding midfield positions.

Here is where the signing of Anderson makes such sense.

Throughout his career, the 23-year-old has played in every midfield and attacking position at one point. For England, he has frequently dropped into defence to form a back five out of possession.

Alongside Rodri, Anderson would be able to sit deep, allowing the Spaniard to showcase his attacking quality - and vice versa.

Both players would be capable of taking turns in dropping deeper to maintain the balance of the team if strong carriers of the ball like Marc Guehi or Josko Gvardiol were to push forward.

Piggy-backing on the success of Rodri's work with Bernardo Silva, City would hope their new versatile and combative winger-turned-holding-midfielder will bring about similar success.

Bouaddi - like Anderson - has played in a number of roles, more specifically holding midfield, right-back and centre-back.

His ability to occupy those positions - with strong defending and elegance on the ball - replicates some of the work Stones did for City.

The club are looking at young and intelligent footballers capable of playing for possession-heavy sides. More important, however, is their ability to be positionally versatile across the roles Maresca's system demands.

When numerous players can move into any of the positions that open up, it can result in a structured yet fluid team that become harder for the opposition to defend against – think Luis Enrique's Paris St-Germain.

But this takes both time and tutelage.

City will look better with Rodri, who possesses an understanding of positioning, speed and risk that Anderson and future signings may take time to grasp.

After all, it took Rodri a few seasons to navigate the change in environment under Fernandinho's wing.

But should he go, Maresca has previously shown an impressive ability to recognise positions players could move into but haven't yet done: Stones into holding midfield, Caicedo into full-back, Marc Cucurella into attacking midfield... the list goes on.

Whether or not City further bolster their squad, Maresca will hope to have a greater number of pieces to place on his board - a departure from Guardiola's approach of maintaining a smaller squad.

That factor - and this holds true whether or not Rodri stays - should give City's new boss a greater chance of landing on a working formula next season.

title: LA Dodgers and MVP Ohtani launch summer of live baseball on BBC
description: World Series champions the Los Angeles Dodgers will launch a summer of live Major League Baseball on the BBC.
fullText:
Defending World Series champions the Los Angeles Dodgers will launch a summer of live Major League Baseball on the BBC when they meet the New York Mets on Sunday.

The Dodgers lead the National League again in 2026, with last season's Most Valuable Player, Shohei Ohtani, to the fore as they target a third consecutive World Series title.

The struggling Mets are in need of inspiration from star man Juan Soto as they look to turn around a difficult start to the season.

The game sets up a run of 10 consecutive live Sunday night MLB matches on the BBC, including the season finale on September 27 before four post-season games the following week.

Why Dodgers are on brink of World Series dynasty

The night the Tartan Army took over iconic Fenway Park

The Dodgers' record of 65 wins and 38 defeats means they are likely to win the National League West for the 13th time in 14th years.

Their recent dominance is built around Ohtani, whose achievements are now compared to the greatest players in the history of the game.

His ability to both hit and pitch at the top level consistently - he already has 22 home runs this year and has recorded eight wins as a pitcher - demonstrates a similar skill-set to the legendary two-way player Babe Ruth.

Ohtani has been named Most Valuable Player in his league four times, including last season, when the Dodgers became the first franchise in 25 years to win consecutive World Series titles.

Dominican left-fielder Soto became the highest-paid player in baseball history in 2024 when he left the New York Yankees and signed a $765m deal with their bitter cross-city rivals the Mets.

He hit his 250th career home run against the Yankees earlier this season, one of 21 home runs he has delivered in 2026.

Despite Soto's contribution, the Mets narrowly missed out on a post-season berth last year and now sit bottom of the National League East with 43 wins to 60 defeats.

This season, the MLB Bases Covered Live team will again be led by play-by-play announcer Melanie Newman, with former St Louis Cardinals first baseman Xavier Scruggs and Maccabees guitarist Felix White alongside to call the action for seasoned baseball fans and new viewers.

During the 2026 Fifa World Cup, baseball played an unexpectedly large role in the experiences of football fans and players from the UK as they enjoyed memorable outings to ballparks across the US.

After defeating Haiti in their opening game in nearby Foxborough, Scotland's Tartan Army took over Fenway Park in Boston to celebrate while watching the Red Sox take on the Texas Rangers.

title: Seven stars to watch at Wafcon 2026 and why
description: As the biggest ever Women's Africa Cup of Nations gets ready for kick-off, BBC Sport Africa picks seven players to keep an eye on in Morocco.
fullText:
The 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon) kicks off on Sunday, with Nigeria defending their title.

Morocco is hosting for the third time in a row, with the Atlas Lionesses aiming to lift the trophy for the first time after losing back-to-back finals on home soil.

This year's tournament has added importance because qualification for the 2027 Fifa Women's World Cup is on the line, with the four semi-finalists securing a ticket to Brazil.

BBC Sport Africa picks out seven players to watch.

The AFC Toronto forward was the inspiration behind her country's run to a record-extending 10th title last year with two goals and six assists.

Seizing her moment as a starter from the quarter-finals onwards, Okoronkwo combined creativity with some unerring finishing.

With the Super Falcons trailing 2-0 against the hosts in the final, it was the 29-year-old's composed penalty which sparked the comeback.

Okoronkwo then set up Folashade Ijamilusi's equaliser and Jennifier Echegini's late winner to complete a remarkable turnaround.

Despite her impact, Okoronkwo was surprisingly overlooked at the Confederation of African Football awards last year, meaning she may have extra motivation to show what she can do on the big stage.

Malawi are one of two Wafcon debutants and the Lyon forward is the main goal threat for the lowest-ranked nation at the finals, having helped fire her club side to a fifth consecutive league title in France last season.

In 2023, while at Paris St-Germain, she became the first Malawian woman to play and score in the Uefa Champions League.

The 30-year-old is expected to line up in attack alongside younger sister Temwa as the scorchers face a tough group containing Nigeria, Zambia and Egypt.

"I was waiting to qualify for the Africa Cup of Nations [for] a long time," she said.

"I've been playing big games in Europe, but I like to tell the girls 'don't be shy, don't be scared'.

"We can't wait to start and see what we can do."

Is this the final chance for the Atlas Lionesses captain to lift the trophy?

The 35-year-old opened the scoring against Nigeria in last year's final but Morocco were ultimately forced to settle for silver medals again.

Chebbak did pick up the golden boot, netting five times, having been joint top scorer in 2022 when South Africa thwarted Morocco in the final.

And the Al-Hilal forward, who was named African player of the year in November, is also bidding for another unique piece of history.

Her father Larbi helped Morocco to the men's Africa Cup of Nations title in 1976, and Chebbak will hope it is third time lucky for her as she targets a unique double.

The form of the Harambee Starlets goalkeeper will be crucial if the East Africans are to surprise people and make the knockout stage.

Awuor played a vital role in helping Kenya back to the finals for the first time since 2016, saving two penalties in the second leg of their first-round qualifying tie away against Tunisia last February.

The 27-year-old has gained experience since her move to Romanian side Farul Constanta two years ago, helping them secure back-to-back league titles.

Kenya, the second lowest-ranked side at the finals at 128th in the world, take on Morocco, Algeria and Senegal in a tricky Group A.

Ghazi was just 14 the last time Egypt appeared at Wafcon – but was still included in the Cleopatras squad for that tournament in 2016, even if she did not make it on to the pitch.

With a decade of extra experience under her belt, the Al Ahly midfielder, who has battled hard to return to her best after rupturing an anterior cruciate ligament three years ago, is taking inspiration from Egypt's men and their run to the last 16 at the 2026 Fifa World Cup.

"This is the best motivation we could ever get for our women's team," Ghazi said.

"They've filled our hearts with so much joy.

"We have a big responsibility to inspire and keep moving the legacy of Egyptian women's football, especially on the African stage."

Firmly established as one of South Africa's senior leaders, Banyana Banyana's skipper will be looking to help her team reclaim the title they won for the first time in 2022.

"When you look at the number of teams in this year's edition, I think this will be one of the most challenging tournaments we've ever had in the history of Wafcon," said the 33-year-old midfielder, who recently joined an elite group by winning her 150th cap.

At a minimum, South Africa will be looking to reach the last four again, which would guarantee Desiree Ellis' team a place at a third successive World Cup, having reached the last 16 at the 2023 tournament in Australia and New Zealand.

"[The coaching staff] have experienced the team winning the Wafcon and not doing so well. We've got the recipe that you need in order to succeed," Jane added.

South Africa have been drawn alongside Tanzania, Ivory Coast and Burkina Faso in Group B.

The other debutants at this year's finals are Cape Verde, whose women only played their first international in 2018.

Da Luz has been part of the squad since the early days and assumed the captaincy in 2020.

The left-back, who has a degree in systems and computer engineering, leads a side consisting entirely of part-time players.

A serial title winner with Praia-based Seven Stars, Da Luz popped up with two vital goals in qualifying.

She netted in both legs in the first round, a 6-3 aggregate win over Guinea, before the islanders secured their spot on the road in Bamako where they upset Mali, who they will face again after the Eagles also progressed to the finals based on their world ranking.

title: 'We wanted to be Bournemouth' - Rose begins Cherries reign with win
description: Marco Rose kicked off his Bournemouth reign with a 4-1 victory over German side St. Pauli in the Cherries' opening pre-season fixture.  Rose's side fell a goal behind in the first half, but goals from Ben Gannon-Doak, Harold William, Daniel Jebbison and Bafode Diakite helped Bournemouth seal a victory in Saalfelden, Austria.  Speaking to BBC Radio Solent, the Cherries boss said he was "pleased" with the result and that he was content with the performance from his players.
fullText:
Marco Rose kicked off his Bournemouth reign with a 4-1 victory over German side St. Pauli in the Cherries' opening pre-season fixture.

Rose's side fell a goal behind in the first half, but goals from Ben Gannon-Doak, Harold William, Daniel Jebbison and Bafode Diakite helped Bournemouth seal a victory in Saalfelden, Austria.

Speaking to BBC Radio Solent, the Cherries boss said he was "pleased" with the result and that he was content with the performance from his players.

"I saw many good things, but it is good to have a first game with footage and work on things that we need to improve.

"We wanted to be Bournemouth, and we wanted to be proactive, and I think that is what we saw today," said Rose.

Alex Scott, who has been linked with a move away from Bournemouth, featured, but Eli Junior Kroupi did not play due to a lack of training.

When asked about the speculation which surrounds Scott and Kroupi, Rose said: "I am not here to comment on any rumours or things like this."

Although Rose declined to comment on potential outgoings at Bournemouth, he said it was "not a secret" that the south coast side are aiming to sign defender, Antonio Silva from Benfica.

"We want this player, the player wants to join us and the clubs are in talks – that's nothing new. Now we are waiting for him," added Rose.

title: LA Dodgers and MVP Ohtani launch summer of live baseball on BBC
description: World Series champions the Los Angeles Dodgers will launch a summer of live Major League Baseball on the BBC.
fullText:
Defending World Series champions the Los Angeles Dodgers will launch a summer of live Major League Baseball on the BBC when they meet the New York Mets on Sunday.

The Dodgers lead the National League again in 2026, with last season's Most Valuable Player, Shohei Ohtani, to the fore as they target a third consecutive World Series title.

The struggling Mets are in need of inspiration from star man Juan Soto as they look to turn around a difficult start to the season.

The game sets up a run of 10 consecutive live Sunday night MLB matches on the BBC, including the season finale on September 27 before four post-season games the following week.

Why Dodgers are on brink of World Series dynasty

The night the Tartan Army took over iconic Fenway Park

The Dodgers' record of 65 wins and 38 defeats means they are likely to win the National League West for the 13th time in 14th years.

Their recent dominance is built around Ohtani, whose achievements are now compared to the greatest players in the history of the game.

His ability to both hit and pitch at the top level consistently - he already has 22 home runs this year and has recorded eight wins as a pitcher - demonstrates a similar skill-set to the legendary two-way player Babe Ruth.

Ohtani has been named Most Valuable Player in his league four times, including last season, when the Dodgers became the first franchise in 25 years to win consecutive World Series titles.

Dominican left-fielder Soto became the highest-paid player in baseball history in 2024 when he left the New York Yankees and signed a $765m deal with their bitter cross-city rivals the Mets.

He hit his 250th career home run against the Yankees earlier this season, one of 21 home runs he has delivered in 2026.

Despite Soto's contribution, the Mets narrowly missed out on a post-season berth last year and now sit bottom of the National League East with 43 wins to 60 defeats.

This season, the MLB Bases Covered Live team will again be led by play-by-play announcer Melanie Newman, with former St Louis Cardinals first baseman Xavier Scruggs and Maccabees guitarist Felix White alongside to call the action for seasoned baseball fans and new viewers.

During the 2026 Fifa World Cup, baseball played an unexpectedly large role in the experiences of football fans and players from the UK as they enjoyed memorable outings to ballparks across the US.

After defeating Haiti in their opening game in nearby Foxborough, Scotland's Tartan Army took over Fenway Park in Boston to celebrate while watching the Red Sox take on the Texas Rangers.

title: Why is it so special to be part of Team Scotland?
description: Competing for Scotland is a rare opportunity. BBC Scotland takes a look at why it means so much.
fullText:
There's the girl you know from your home town. The boy you went to university with. The fella who trains in the same gym as you every day. And your best pal and training partner is there, too.

None of you are having to speak slowly, to clip your Rs, or accentuate your vowels. You understand the patter, know what square sausage is, and can fluently punctuate by swearing.

It's like being among family and friends, with all the tender aggression and familiar hinterland that brings.

That is the atmosphere within Team Scotland, a diverse - yet similar - collection of athletes and staff who represent the country once every four years at the Commonwealth Games and will do so again in Glasgow in 2026.

"There's just something about being Scottish - we all just get it and that identity really resonates with us," says swimmer and Olympic and Commonwealth Games veteran Ross Murdoch.

"It's a completely different dynamic to Team GB. Everyone's just… it's a breath of fresh air," adds Olympic silver and bronze-winning cyclist Jack Carlin.

"It's warmer and more intimate," says Commonwealth badminton medallist Kirsty Gilmour. "With GB, you need to put your extrovert mask on and try to make new friends, but you just feel more at ease in Team Scotland."

Scotland agrees to host Commonwealth Games in 2026

What do athletes think about Glasgow 2026?

Those three athletes have also competed regularly for Britain and are at pains to make it clear that they enjoy, and even relish, doing so. But the Commonwealths are a rare chance to represent Scotland. Their country. Where they are from.

For most, the divergence is not political either. Instead, it is something far less tangible. A feeling. That's why explaining it isn't easy, particular for people whose sporting talents are their primary means of expression.

Ask athletes why it is special to represent Scotland and most immediately reach for the rarity of the opportunity.

In some sports, it only happens once every four years.

But there must be more to it than that? Not least because the Commonwealths lacks a little of the cachet of other events.

"Something just feels different when you're running for Scotland," says distance runner Eilish McColgan, who won a stunning gold medal in the Women's 10,000m in Birmingham in 2022.

"It's like I'm representing my home town - Dundee - a little bit more.

"You're around people you've known since you were wee - the athletes you've grown up with, the coaches, the support staff. And, when you were young, it wasn't about running for GB. It was about running for Scotland. So it just reminds you of home."

The feeling is rooted in childhood for Murdoch, too.

"Just putting on the Scotland kit brings me back to being a wee boy," he says. "I'm from a wee estate in the Vale of Leven and I remember watching Scotland winning medals at the 2006 Commonwealths and that seemed as big as the world could get.

"From then on, that was all I wanted to do, so for this hobby of mine to get totally out of hand and me do this three times… I can't even put that into words."

Hammer thrower Mark Dry has - like Murdoch, Carlin, McColgan and Gilmour - been to Olympics and world championships and is "proud" to have represented Britain. But none of those occasions, while materially more illustrious, have made him feel "anything like competing for Scotland does".

"It means everything to me," he says. "Other championships, you're doing it for yourself, but at the Commonwealths, you're doing it for Scotland."

Boxer Reese Lynch, who made his Games debut in Birmingham, is of a similar mind. "Even when I'm competing for GB, I'm still representing Scotland," he says. "It's where I'm from and it's who I am."

The identity is one aspect of it then. But the environment plays a part, too.

Being inside the Team GB machine at an Olympics can be a stifling, lonely and isolated experience. It is a very serious business, where everyone has "their game-face on", according to Gilmour.

Given these are athletes at the very pinnacle of their sport, that is perhaps how it should be. But it is also telling how many athletes will mention the atmosphere inside the Team Scotland camp as being something they crave every four years.

"For me, it's really good fun," says swimmer Duncan Scott, Scotland's most decorated Games athlete.

That's not to say that the business of winning medals is taken lightly, though. "It's more of a fun rivalry," says veteran Para-cyclist Neil Fachie.

"You've got your British team-mates there, and the Australians seem to get up for it a bit more, but the stress level is slightly lower, and the fun's a bit higher."

"There's no pressure," adds wheelchair racer Sammi Kinghorn. "There is such a spread of athletes and abilities and we are all so grateful to be there. If you win a medal, you come back to the village and everyone is so excited for you."

"It's what I'd call hype vibes," says Olympic shooter Seonaid McIntosh. "Because it's a smaller team than GB, we all know each other and want everyone else to have success. That's a really lovely culture and environment to be in."

Perhaps the greatest testimony to that atmosphere is not from those who were born and raised in Scotland but rather from those who choose to identify as Scots.

Take wrestler Christelle Lemofack. She competed for Cameroon at Glasgow 2014 but enjoyed the experience so much that she never went home. In Birmingham, she represented Scotland.

"I've made a life here and Scotland gave me that opportunity, so I feel like I have to give something back," she said before the last Games. "I've dreamed about this and now it's come true. I have to fight for my new flag."

Lemofack might not have the ginger hair that Olympic judoka Sarah Adlington boasts as part of her credentials to compete for Scotland, but elements of their stories are the same.

"You can't choose where you were born, but you can choose where you live and I've chosen to live my whole adult life in Scotland," says the 2014 Commonwealth gold medallist. "I feel Scottish, my coaches and team-mates are Scottish and I wouldn't want to compete for anyone else."

This article was originally published on 27 July 2022.

title: What's working - and what's not - for WSL fans?
description: BBC Sport spoke to fans of the Women's Super League and England Lionesses to learn about their experiences in the game and discuss what could be improved.
fullText:
"Attendance FC? That's your insult? You're jealous!"

Rachel Major regularly finds herself fending off jibes from rival fans towards Arsenal's growing attendances. A supporter of 20 years, she has enjoyed a prime seat at the club that is driving the growth of the women's game.

Last season, the Gunners averaged 34,000 at Emirates Stadium, almost four times the next highest average attendance which was set by Chelsea - and better than eight Premier League clubs., external

Arsenal's home crowds accounted for 41% of all supporters at WSL fixtures, a club success story, though one that raises questions about the overall supporter experience as both league and clubs strive to progress.

To investigate, BBC Sport asked fans how the game can keep existing followers engaged, captivate new supporters and inspire the next generation.

In January 2026, a YouGov study, external found 28.5m fans of WSL football globally, split equally by gender with almost half aged 18-34.

It is notably different from the men's game, which skews male and older.

"At a men's game, you feel like you're just a cog," says Donna Jones, a season ticket-holder at London City Lionesses. "The game doesn't care about the fans. In the women's game, the players and staff want to build a relationship."

Bankrolled by billionaire majority owner Michele Kang, London City are the only fully independent WSL club and averaged a home crowd of just under 3,000 at League One Bromley's Copperjax Community Stadium in their top-flight debut.

Their efforts to entice new supporters earned the Best Fan Engagement prize at the 2026 Women's Football Awards., external

"The club have done a fantastic job at creating an environment that's not just about the match," adds Jones. "They have different food options, a T-shirt cannon, foam fingers, player signings, a spin-the-wheel at half-time - there is so much.

"They are really trying to grow the fanbase."

The family-friendly hallmark of the women's game has been critical to its growth in England, whose back-to-back victories at the European Championships in 2022 and 2025 ignited an explosion of interest.

Pre-match activities planned for the Wembley fan park before England's fixture against Spain in April encouraged Mark Jenkins to take his six-year-old daughters to their first professional match.

"We did a lot of research in terms of what time to turn up and what would be going on - it was a really good atmosphere in the fan park," he tells BBC Sport. "[My daughters] enjoyed it and the first thing they said was, 'Can we do it again?'

"Women's sport is more accessible now. Eventually they will know the players' names and have posters on the wall just as I had."

The women's game has trialled a fan choice pilot, external over the past two seasons, permitting alcohol to be consumed in the stands.

Adopted by 18 clubs across the WSL and WSL2, it has been well received, with 70% of supporters now in favour, external of the initiative.

"It's absolutely brilliant," affirms Arsenal season ticket-holder Major. "People are better behaved.

"Before, you had 15 minutes to get in the queue, to buy a drink and then down it before you got in. That can promote irresponsible drinking."

The head of women's football at the Football Supporters' Association, Deborah Dilworth, says this is one of many strategies to enhance the matchday experience.

"The fan choice pilot is something that we've supported but this isn't the only part," she explains. "You need to look at food. You need to look at people going into the stadium, where they're walking, how comfortable they feel and how safe they feel."

With attendances increasing, there has been a drive to create separate seating areas to accommodate both avid match-goers and casual followers.

"As different seating sections have been distinguished, there has been a drive to make it clear as to where and what each ticket is," Dilworth explains.

"Home clubs need to have a vibrant section to create an atmosphere but equally there are new fans, neutrals and families."

WSL clubs to provide alcohol at games after trials

The biggest complaint from fans is scheduling.

In 2025-26, the WSL replaced the Sunday 18:45 kick-off time with more noon matches, but this also proved unpopular.

"For an away day it's horrible," explains Arsenal fan Major. "You've got fans leaving at three o'clock in the morning or you're going the night before and having to pay for a hotel."

The revised time also clashes with grassroots football, played widely on a Sunday morning. It is a barrier for the younger generation to attend games.

Regular breaks throughout the season are an issue too. Earlier this year, former England defender Anita Asante suggested extended gaps between league games hampers momentum and rhythm for fans.

Another complaint from supporters is accessibility.

While Premier League-level grounds like Emirates Stadium and Everton's Goodison Park are well equipped, smaller venues are less accommodating.

Jones, a wheelchair user, was frustrated by the lack of Blue Badge parking information when trying to attend London City's away trip to Tottenham Hotspur.

"A lot of the issues I experience are with communication," she says. "Every club has an accessibility section on their website but for Tottenham it is only for the Tottenham Hotspur stadium, not Brisbane Road [where Tottenham women play]."

Jones told BBC Sport the onus was on her to seek further information via email, to which she received a reply stating Blue Badge parking had sold out. Only after she spoke to Tottenham's disability co-ordinator did she learn the venue did not have Blue Badge parking as it was in a residential area.

To compound matters, the wheelchair accessible allocation was on the opposite side of the ground to the away section, leaving Jones isolated.

Tottenham Hotspur told BBC Sport information for the venue is available on the website via the 'Ask Spurs' chatbot. However, after an internal investigation, they are making improvements.

Brisbane Road-specific guidance has since been added to their event day accessible parking section on 'Ask Spurs', while a matchday-specific guide is in the works.

A spokesperson for the club confirmed: "We're working on a full Brisbane Road matchday guide for the website for next season to give parity with our Tottenham Hotspur Stadium information."

Smaller stadiums pose further difficulties given lower quality facilities on offer, larger distances to travel and more complex journeys to navigate.

Major, who travels home and away with Arsenal, highlighted unfavourable conditions when visiting West Ham's Chigwell Construction Stadium, shared with National League club Dagenham & Redbridge.

"There are no seats so if there's someone who is less able to stand, if they're old, if they're injured, if they're disabled, it's not a good experience," she says.

"The whole stand is not covered. It's not a problem in the summer, but [in winter] people are out in the rain."

For most WSL teams, a key strategy to grow their fanbase is to capture the interest of fans already invested in the men's side.

Manchester City and Arsenal held parades at the end of 2025-26 to celebrate the successes of their women's, men's and academy sides.

Gunners fan Major highlights the use of "real fans" in promotional campaigns as an example of the club's ongoing efforts to foster a collective identity.

There are pitfalls to aligning too closely however, as Reading and Charlton Athletic have previously discovered. In 2024, the Royals were demoted from tier two to tier five after the club fell into financial difficulty, while the Addicks were disbanded entirely in 2007 after the men's team suffered relegation.

Next season, Charlton will play top-flight football for the first time since that era.

It means Dilworth at the Football Supporters Association is cautious about clubs simply seeking to "copy and paste from the men's game".

"Are there opportunities to do things differently?" she asks. "Everybody's desperately trying to do the right thing. Innovation is key but not to potentially compromise what people really love about the game."

Another sticking point with the 'one club' approach is the home venue.

"There's something really powerful in the narrative around a stadium for both men's and women's first teams," says Dilworth.

"However, if then beneath that there is still a tone and a culture of the primacy to the men, that's when you run into difficulties."

Brighton's statement answer, erecting Europe's first purpose-built women's football stadium, is one solution, but many WSL clubs do not have the space, money or resources to do likewise.

Brighton plan Europe's first purpose-built £80m women's stadium

Bespoke women's football stadiums? Why US sides are making the move

From next season, Chelsea will play all home WSL fixtures at Stamford Bridge, joining Arsenal, Aston Villa and Everton in committing to home venues with improved transport links and better facilities.

Tottenham, Manchester United and Brighton will host marquee fixtures at their main stadiums, though the majority of matches will be at their smaller grounds.

When it comes to engaging fans when bums are on seats, in stadiums or at home, there is a need to refine communication and marketing strategies.

BBC Sport's 2025 Summer of Sport research revealed social media is the principal way to reach younger audiences, with 35% of 18-24-year-olds using social networks as their primary method of keeping up to date with women's football.

Social media also ranks highly among 25-34-year-old fans, second only to watching live.

"I'll go to social media before Google or somewhere else. Everyone is already talking about it," affirms Major.

WSL fixtures are released on Thursday, 30 July and with the expanded 14-team format, there is potential to draw more eyes than ever in the 2026-27 season.

Then there is the Lionesses factor.

The success and visibility of Sarina Wiegman's side has had a huge impact on fan engagement domestically, with Chloe Kelly's penalty heroics in last summer's Euro 2025 final triumph a "watershed moment" for women's football marketing.

Next summer's World Cup in Brazil will further bolster excitement, though England must navigate two play-off rounds to guarantee their place.

For now, it is over to the clubs to see if they can rectify existing issues and harness the power of the national team to push growth to the next level.

title: The two days which could make or break Fury-AJ
description: BBC Sport looks at how a proposed bout between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua hinges on a 24-hour-period between Friday and Saturday.
fullText:
After more than a decade of posturing and power struggles - a soap opera of warring promoters, shifting managers, fractured television deals and failed negotiations - it has finally come down to this.

The biggest fight in British boxing history - Tyson Fury versus Anthony Joshua - hangs on one final two-day stretch.

On Friday, Fury, 37, fights Mariusz Wach in the unlikely surroundings of Pattaya, Thailand. There is no broadcaster, only a modest crowd expected and a 46-year-old opponent.

The following evening, almost 4,000 miles away in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, Joshua returns against Kristian Prenga - an Albanian knockout artist whom even the most hardened boxing fans would struggle to pick out of a line-up.

If all goes to plan, Fury will leave Thailand within hours of beating Wach, board a private jet and fly to Saudi Arabia, where he is expected to climb through the ropes and finally stand face-to-face with Joshua.

The contracts are signed but, especially in boxing, the ink is never truly dry until the opening bell rings.

Fury lighter than opponent for first time in 15 years

Pre-fight Joshua not ready for death of friends to sink in

'Would Beckham do it?' - Fury stands by Thailand fight

Fury and Joshua, 36, have defined British heavyweight boxing for more than a decade without ever sharing a professional ring.

Yet they arrive at this moment for very different reasons. For Joshua, it is about far more than shaking off ring rust.

The two-time world champion has not fought since surviving the car crash in Nigeria last December that claimed the lives of close friends Sina Ghami and Latif "Latz" Ayodele.

Joshua has spoken about the emotional toll of the tragedy. Promoter Eddie Hearn believes boxing has "saved" Joshua - just as it did when he first took up the sport as a troubled 19-year-old searching for direction.

"When you come off an incident like that and an accident like that, I guess people say, 'Will you ever be the same?' Certainly everything he's shown in training camp, after he went through all the near-impossible work to get himself in that position, shows that he is," Hearn told BBC Sport.

"The questions that you ask yourself, the moments where your head hits the pillow at night and it's just you in your room, what's going on inside between those two ears?"

There was also the physical recovery.

"In the early stages, just a slight movement in bed would be excruciating pain," Hearn said.

"To getting back on the bike and doing two hours' cycling when he couldn't move his upper body, and going through the physio sessions, that was an incredible journey."

Fury, who briefly retired after back-to-back defeats by Oleksandr Usyk, already had the comeback fight many felt he needed when comfortably outpointing Arslanbek Makhmudov in April.

BBC boxing pundit Steve Bunce is not convinced another outing was necessary.

"The fight against Makhmudov was perfect, it was the dream fight for a fighter after a long break," Bunce says.

"You could see he wasn't bothered about the stoppage, he just needed those priceless rounds. But this fight against Wach is one he will not lose under any circumstances. It's ceremonial."

Fury's trip to Thailand appears to be as much about publicity as preparation.

The cameras for the third season of his Netflix documentary, 'At Home with the Furys' will be rolling at ringside with exclusive access. No other broadcaster will be present.

It would rank among the biggest upsets in heavyweight history if Fury lost to a man who turns 47 this year and has lost seven of his past 10 fights.

"Fury should dominate but the biggest risk for me is that he looks awful," Bunce says.

"Also, Tyson might find out that he has lost something and senses some flaws in himself."

There is a fraction more jeopardy for Joshua. Prenga is largely an unknown quantity to the wider public, but his record demands respect: 20 wins, 20 knockouts and one defeat.

"This fight is designed to be competitive, but not too competitive," Hearn says.

"He's never boxed at AJ's level, but until you fight at that level, you actually don't know if you're good enough. But he's decent, he's game and he's dangerous."

The greater threat to the Fury-AJ super-fight is injury.

"Tyson is too smart and clever and I think Wach won't be using his elbows or head. There will be some sort of gentleman's agreement," Bunce adds.

"He could injure his arm or leg. At Tyson's age, with hard training camps, that can happen. It could also happen to Joshua."

If both men emerge unscathed, attention will quickly turn to Jeddah. The hope is that Fury will travel straight from Thailand and join Joshua in the ring for an official announcement.

"Perhaps Fury will get on a private jet and arrive in Jeddah - give it a bit of drama in the style of WWE," Bunce said.

"But if they both win, you have to announce it right then. You can't let it slip."

Remarkably, the two have only ever shared a ring once before - a semi-mythical sparring session back in 2010 when Fury was a 21-year-old prospect with an undefeated professional record and Joshua was a raw 20-year-old amateur.

Hearn is a little less certain Fury will make the journey to Saudi Arabia.

"We hope, now that the contracts are signed, we'll see him on Saturday," Hearn said.

"I would suggest most people would get on a plane, but he is Tyson Fury."

Saudi Arabia powerbroker Turki Alalshikh, a key figure in bringing together Fury v Joshua, has said that for the fight to happen on British soil, it would require a middle-of-the-night start time at Wembley Stadium to cater for prime-time American audiences on Netflix.

Such a plan would require extending Wembley's usual 11pm curfew, although sources close to London Mayor Sadiq Khan indicated the city would be willing to help make it happen.

Industry whispers point towards Las Vegas or New York, while Hearn says Joshua's contract stipulates the fight must happen in the UK - but he has not ruled out a move to America.

The prospect of the biggest British fight in history taking place thousands of miles away is a difficult one for many UK fans to accept.

Whatever unfolds across these extraordinary coming hours, we are about to find out whether the biggest fight in British boxing history is going to be a reality or destined to remain the sport's greatest what-if.

title: Potter and Yee among favourites at World Triathlon London event
description: Alex Yee and Beth Potter compete at the World Triathlon Championship Series in London this weekend, and you can follow the action live on the BBC.
fullText:
World Triathlon Championship Series: London

Live on BBC iPlayer and BBC Sport website and app

Olympic medallists Alex Yee and Beth Potter will be competing at the World Triathlon Championship Series in London this weekend, and you can follow the action live on the BBC.

Paris 2024 gold medallist Yee returns after competing in marathons and more recently, the 5,000m in the Monaco Diamond League.

Fellow Briton Potter tops the women's standings and world rankings after three podium places in the opening rounds of the series.

The WTCS represents the flagship elite series of World Triathlon, with the world's best triathletes competing at iconic venues including the ExCeL London.

A further three races are planned for the season, which culminates with the finals in Pontevedra, Spain, in September.

Potter will be among the favourites to win on British soil, despite missing June's Quiberon race in France because of altitude training and finishing sixth in the previous meeting in Hamburg.

The Glaswegian, who claimed bronze in the Paris 2024 Olympics, won the season opener in Uzbekistan and came second in both the Japan and Sardinia races.

Since delivering one of the standout moments of the Paris Games, Yee has experimented with marathon running – making his debut in the London 2025 race and then achieving the second-fastest time by a Briton in Valencia 2025, running 2:06:38.

The 28-year-old began his transition back to triathlon in Yokohama where he finished fifth. But the Olympic champion failed to finish the men's race in Sardinia.

Jeanne Lehair - Luxemburg: Lehair has finished third in the first two races of the season and currently holds second place in the WTS standings.

Lisa Tertsch - Germany: Tertsch is ranked second in the world and led the series coming into Hamburg but was pipped to the post by France's Leonie Periault.

Georgia Taylor-Brown - Great Britain: The Manchester-born athlete has won bronze in the 2018 and 2019 World Triathlon Series and won the one-off sprint triathlon race in Hamburg to become the 2020 World Triathlon Champion. She has also won individual silver at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics and gold in the mixed team relay. She is in ninth place in the current standings.

Vasco Vilaca - Portugal: With two first and second-place finishes, Vilaca is proving to be the man to beat. He is yet to add a title to his medal collection but he leads both the World and Series standings.

Miguel Hidalgo - Brazil: Hidalgo was disqualified from the Hamburg race because he did not serve a 10-second penalty during the race for altering the race number on his cycling bib.

Oliver Conway - Great Britain: Conway made is debut in the WTCS last year and won the U23 Championship. He is just outside the top 10 in 11th place, having shown promise by finishing fifth in the season opener.

title: The Bezos factor - unpicking puzzle of Liverpool's potential investors
description: Could Amazon founder and American billionaire Jeff Bezos really become one of Liverpool's new investors? BBC Sport takes a look.
fullText:
The story of potential investment in Liverpool took a new twist on Wednesday, as Jeff Bezos' name was thrown into the mix.

Barely 24 hours earlier, it had emerged that a consortium led by British-Indian millionaire businessman Amit Bhatia had expressed interest in buying a stake in the Premier League club.

Normally at this time of year, attention is focused on transfer activity before the new season.

But when Liverpool's owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG) confirmed Bhatia's interest in exploring the possibility of acquiring a "strategic minority investment" in the club, it generated the kind of interest and conversation among supporters typically reserved for a marquee signing.

The 46-year-old, the son-in-law of the Indian billionaire businessman Lakshmi Mittal, had been a director and co-owner of Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before relinquishing his stake in the club on Tuesday.

His decision to step away from the west London club appears to pave the way for him to lead a consortium of investors seeking to purchase a reported 30% stake in the Anfield club.

Now new reports suggest Amazon founder Bezos has been approached about joining the consortium.

Sources close to Bhatia declined to comment when asked by BBC Sport whether Bezos had been approached, saying only that the consortium had held discussions with a number of potential investors. FSG also declined to comment.

BBC Sport takes a look at Bezos' background and whether the American businessman could be about to become part of the Premier League's world.

American businessman Bezos, founder of e-commerce giant Amazon, is the fourth-richest person in the world.

According to Forbes, the 62-year-old has an estimated net worth of $256.9bn (£192.1bn).

He stepped down as Amazon's chief executive in 2021 to become executive chairman, although he still owns 8% of the company.

Bezos also owns The Washington Post and aerospace company Blue Origin and, as recently as 2021, was ranked as the world's richest person.

Although Bezos has yet to invest in sport, he has come close on more than one occasion.

In 2023, the American billionaire was linked with a takeover of NFL franchise the Washington Commanders after owner Daniel Snyder put the team up for sale.

He has also previously explored the possibility of buying Super Bowl winners the Seattle Seahawks.

Bezos ultimately decided against submitting an offer for either franchise.

When FSG sold a minority single-figure percentage stake to global sports investment firm Dynasty Equity in 2023, that deal allowed it to make up on revenue lost during the pandemic and pay down debt for projects such as investment in the club's training centre in Kirkby and the Anfield Road stand expansion.

This time around, that is not the case - the club are in a strong position financially. In February, Liverpool confirmed that they achieved record revenues of more than £700m and was the highest-placed Premier League club in the Deloitte Football Money League.

So this development certainly raises questions about the long-term future of FSG. From an FSG perspective, it has seen Liverpool win everything there is to win since buying the club in 2010 for £300m, while upgrading the training ground and developing the stadium. According to the Financial Times, a deal with the Bhatia consortium would value the club at around £4.5bn. So perhaps FSG believes the club is peaking and it may be time to start stepping away.

This is an uncertain time for Liverpool with a new head coach in Andoni Iraola and big changes at senior level, with Michael Edwards stepping down as FSG's CEO of football, primarily because the ownership had moved away from the idea of investing in other football clubs. Meanwhile, Liverpool sporting director Richard Hughes has been strongly linked with a move to Al Hilal in Saudi Arabia.

For now, Liverpool supporters are left with more questions than answers.

Since completing its takeover of the club in October 2010, Fenway Sports Group, then known as New England Sports Ventures, has established itself as a steady and reliable custodian.

The American ownership group has overseen sustained success on and off the pitch, with Liverpool winning two Premier League titles, the Champions League, FA Cup, League Cup, Super Cup and Club World Cup since 2019.

Therefore, the prospect of new investors, and potentially new ideas and approaches, inevitably raises questions, particularly if they are entering elite-level sport for the first time.

Liverpool supporter Neil Atkinson, CEO of The Anfield Wrap, told BBC Sport that questions "should be asked whenever anyone is interested in paying money for an involvement in any Premier League club".

He said: "What is in it for these very, very wealthy individuals, for whom Liverpool's yearly turnover, not profit, which is rare for Premier League clubs, would barely make a dent?

"The 'why' won't be one thing or the same across the board. Part-ownership in four or five sports across the globe could have been deemed to have more value for the Mittal family than partnerships, for instance. At least here you still hold the value of the asset.

"However, as long as everyone keeps asking the 'why' at such an expensive price point, then we will hopefully understand the motive more at some stage."

Almost four years after FSG explored the possibility of selling the 20-time English champions, the prospect of new investors raises the question of whether this could be part of a longer-term strategy towards an eventual exit from Anfield.

title: Where are Newcastle in bid to be the best by 2030?
description: As the fifth anniversary of Newcastle's takeover approaches, BBC Sport assesses whether the project to be "the best" is still on track.
fullText:
Three years, seven months and 21 days.

That is how long it took for Manchester City to win their first Premier League title following the club's takeover by the Abu Dhabi United Group in 2008.

Memories of such a relatively swift transformation were still fresh in the minds of top-flight executives after Newcastle United's Saudi-led buyout in 2021.

"There was quite a lot of fear in the other clubs because they thought it was going to be another Manchester City," a source said.

The reality proved a little different.

Newcastle may have gone on to end a 70-year wait for a major domestic trophy by lifting the EFL Cup in 2025.

Eddie Howe's side may have qualified for the Champions League in 2023 and 2025.

But the regulatory landscape has changed dramatically since Manchester City first set out to disrupt the established order, as football finance expert Kieran Maguire succinctly explained.

"The challenge for Newcastle United is in the era of PSR (profit and sustainability rules) and now SCR (squad-cost ratio), it is very much geared towards preserving the status quo," he said.

Newcastle, nonetheless, had big ambitions from the outset.

They may have been in deep relegation trouble at the time, but former owner Amanda Staveley made it clear in her opening round of interviews that the club's aim was to win the Premier League within a decade.

There was a concern elsewhere in the top flight that Newcastle could look to finance such a push within the rules by turbocharging revenues through lucrative sponsorship deals with Saudi companies.

As BBC Sport previously reported, an unnamed executive contacted the Premier League on behalf of his club and 10 others just a few days after the buyout.

He requested that notice was given of a vote to introduce a short-term ban on such related-party transactions.

This was the precursor to the rules on associated party transactions (APTs), which were introduced in December 2021.

Newcastle's income streams have still grown - from £140m in 2021 to £335.3m in 2025 - but they are lagging behind the Premier League's highest-earning clubs.

Newcastle may only be two places below sixth-placed Chelsea in the top-flight's revenue table, but the Blues still generated £155m 

This is just one of the reasons why Chelsea have been able to agree a club-record £117m deal with Aston Villa for Morgan Rogers and hand the England forward a sizeable wage increase.

As the fifth anniversary of the takeover approaches in October, Newcastle clearly have work to do on and off the field.

Chairman Yasir Al-Rumayyan set out to be "number one" while chief executive David Hopkinson's aim was to be "in the debate about being the top club in the world" by 2030.

But Newcastle need the infrastructure to match.

An announcement is awaited on plans for a new state-of-the-art training ground after a site was identified in Woolsington near Newcastle Airport.

The club have stressed the importance of taking time to make the right decision when it comes to either expanding St James' Park or building a new stadium, which will be key to boosting revenue.

To consistently compete, however, there is little margin for error.

Newcastle needed to see more of an immediate return from a £100m-plus net spend last summer, for example, but defender Malick Thiaw has been the only unquestioned success.

The club are also counting the cost of a bruising 12th-placed finish last season after missing out on Europe.

Most pertinently, after breaching Uefa's financial sustainability regulations, Newcastle have entered into a three-year settlement with European football's governing body.

Raising funds through the sales of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali to Barcelona and Tottenham Hotspur respectively was therefore crucial in order for the club to have the ability to reinvest this summer.

Three key players have now left in less than 12 months, though, which has weakened the side considerably, following Alexander Isak's painful £125m departure to Liverpool last summer.

Newcastle do not want to lose another big name in Bruno Guimaraes, but the captain's future is uncertain after he intimated he wished to join Arsenal.

Whatever happens, trading will remain a key part of the club's strategy in the coming years and there has been a shift in approach with incomings too.

Further reinforcements are sorely needed but all of the club's arrivals this summer - goalkeeper Ewen Jaouen, midfielder Sean Steur and winger Bazoumana Toure - have been aged 20 and under, and from the continent.

The trio have immense potential and, in the right hands, could flourish, but they will need time. It feels like the same could be said for the project as a whole right now.

title: The carpenter aiming for Commonwealth boxing glory
description: BBC Sport meets Tommy Teers, who is balancing his job as a carpenter with training to box at the 2026 Commonwealth Games for Guernsey.
fullText:
But by night the 28-year-old trains in the gym with the aim of bringing boxing glory to Guernsey at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

"I started boxing just to keep fit and to get to this stage is crazy," Teers tells BBC Guernsey as he take a break from training in the gym.

"I've put the hard work in and everyone around me has supported me, so I feel like it's time."

But the hard work for Teers is not just confined to the gym, it is what he does during the day as he balances his sport and carpentry.

Guernsey select team for 2026 Commonwealth Games

He boxes three nights a week, does strength and conditioning every night in-between before either doing sprints or a long run at the weekend.

"It's hard balancing everything, but I'm doing what I can," he says.

"The guys I'll be fighting, they're full-time athletes, but I can't afford to do that.

"I've got my business to run and that's kind of what I want to do, so doing this will be a good experience for me to see what level I can actually get to."

Teers and Niall Adams will fight for Guernsey as part of their 20-strong team going to Glasgow.

The bantamweight has twice reached the English Elite National semi-finals and has fought Ellis Trowbridge, who has been selected to represent England in Glasgow.

"I'm just going to give it my all, perform as best as I can that's all I can ask for really," he says.

"I know the competition's going to be hard, it's definitely a step up for me.

"But that's what I want, I want to see how good I can get and how I can compete against those guys."

title: 'Thank you for all the unforgettable memories' - Anderson says goodbye
description: Elliot Anderson has posted an emotional goodbye to Nottingham Forest as he prepares to join Manchester City.  Earlier in July, City confirmed an agreement has been reached to sign Anderson, stating the "formalities of the move will be finalised upon his return to England" after the World Cup.  BBC Sport reported a deal had been put in place on 25 June.
fullText:
Elliot Anderson has posted an emotional goodbye to Nottingham Forest as he prepares to join Manchester City.

Earlier in July, City confirmed an agreement has been reached to sign Anderson, stating the "formalities of the move will be finalised upon his return to England" after the World Cup. BBC Sport reported a deal had been put in place on 25 June.

The 23-year-old made 92 appearances across two seasons at Forest after joining from boyhood club Newcastle in 2024, helping them qualify for Europe in 2024-25 and reach the Europa League semi-finals the following year.

The goodbye message posted by Anderson on social media read: "Forest family,

"Firstly I am so grateful for the love and support you have shown me over the last 2 years especially towards the end of this season. From the minute I walked through the door I fell in love with this club.

"I want to thank Mr Marinakas, the staff and all players for welcoming me and making my time here so enjoyable, this club gave me the opportunity to grow as a player and a person.

"Bringing the club European football again after 29 years is what all of you fans deserved and to be a helping hand in that is so special.

"Nottingham forest will always have a special place in my heart. Thank you for all the unforgettable memories."

title: Heptathlete Woodward ready to make Jersey history
description: BBC Sport meets Lucy Woodward, the first-ever heptathlete to represent Jersey at the Commonwealth Games.
fullText:
"I'm just a Jack of all trades," jokes Lucy Woodward as she trains at Jersey's athletics track for the final time before the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

The 23-year-old is set to make history in Glasgow as the first woman from Jersey to compete in a multi-event discipline in the heptathlon later this week.

She is part of a five-strong athletics team from Jersey which sees decathlete Evan Campbell joined by sprinters Zach Saunders, Steve MacKay and Jamie Oldham.

"I don't have any standout events, I always thought if I was good enough at something it might be an easier life to specialise," she tells BBC Jersey at the FB Fields athletics track where she first started multi-eventing aged 10.

"I just think the training is so diverse, every day is different. I like that you can have one bad event and then you can make up for it and it's the most interesting event if you ask me."

Glasgow 2026 'a dream come true' for Jersey's Woodward

Nowacki heads Jersey's 2026 Commonwealth Games team

In an event where being a full-time athlete is a huge advantage, Woodward has to balance her training with a full-time job as an architect in London.

It means training six days a week on top of a full-time job and using any spare holidays for competitions, but it is a life she relishes.

"I've grown up balancing this my whole life through A-levels, GCSEs, university and it just kind of becomes a part of like who you are, part of my routine," she added.

"My coaches are very accommodating and they often do very late days at the track waiting for me to finish work.

"I think the thing with me is I really love my job and I really love my training, so if you love both things just as much then the long days and lack of downtime are worth it."

Qualifying for a heptathlon at a major games is not easy.

Unlike individual events there are not many heptathlons at the required standard that you can compete in, making opportunities to reach the qualifying mark few and far between.

Woodward had to travel to Germany in May to find a suitable event where she scored a personal best of 5391 - just short of the 5400 she needed.

"Going into that weekend I was going 'I have to pretty much ace every event to get this standard and that's the only opportunity I have'," she said.

"The whole way through the competition I was like 'I did this event, now I'm recalculating my score to figure out what I need to do', and then ultimately it came down to I had to run a really fast 800m because I messed up my javelin.

"I still did a huge PB, but after javelin I was faced with the situation of to get 5,300 points I have to run quicker than 2:17 and to get 5,400 I have to run 2:10 and my PB was 2.13.

"So that is a pretty stressful environment to be in and I was running it on my own as none of the girls had a PB lower than 2:18.

"But I crossed the line in 2:11 and that is probably the most proud I've ever been of the way that I ran that race.

"I hadn't got the standard, but I was pretty sure I'd proved myself enough, so it was sit and wait and hope that it was enough."

It proved to be enough and a few weeks later she got confirmation that she would be selected for the Jersey team.

It opens up the type of opportunity that rarely comes for athletes from the island - and a first-ever major championships for Woodward.

"This is going to be huge for me, I've never stepped into the stadium full of this many people," she added.

"But ultimately me and my coach were just saying the hard work's done, the most anxiety-inducing thing was probably my qualifying heptathlon where I had one opportunity to get this score and then otherwise I'd have to wait another four years."

So what are Woodward's goals as she prepares to compete against heptathletes including double world champion Katarina Johnson-Thompson, World Championship silver medallist Kate O'Connor and 2022 Commonwealth Games bronze medallist Jade O'Dowda?

"I think I have more long-term targets - ultimately I want to score 6,000, that's a big mark in heptathlon," Woodward added.

"I want to go to the next Commonwealth Games and be more competitive and hopefully get to Gotzis which is a massive heptathlon competition.

"So I'm using Glasgow as kind of like a stepping stone, I just want to go and have the time of my life - which I think I will - hopefully get some good PBs, use the environment, use the girls, they're going to be fast to hopefully carry me to PBs.

"If I can come away with a handful of PBs and an overall heptathlon PB I'll have done my job, and I will be very happy."

title: Five big names to look out for at Glasgow 2026
description: With 215 gold medals up for grabs, across 10 sports at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, BBC Scotland takes a look at some of the biggest names searching for a slab of metal.
fullText:
With 215 golds up for grabs at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, highlighting just five medal hopefuls is no easy feat.

Scotland's largest city is set to welcome more than 3,000 athletes from 10 sports, all of whom have the ambition of leaving with a slab of metal resting on their chest.

For some, a podium-finish is paramount. The bare minimum. For others, competing at the Games is a win in itself.

Much has been made of the reduced programme, the city's readiness and the 'what next?' once Glasgow has passed on the hosting baton again, but for now, the attention - finally - is fully on the athletes.

Here, BBC Scotland takes a look at some of the biggest names battling it out in the upcoming Commonwealth Games.

Is Glasgow ready for the Commonwealth Games - and does the city care?

Can Wales find new Commonwealth legends in Glasgow?

Keep up to date with the Commonwealth Games here

We couldn't start with anyone else, could we?

Even before he walked the walk after talking the talk, new mile world-record holder Josh Kerr was pictured as the poster boy for his home Games.

The brazen - arguably gallus - boy from Edinburgh has won the hearts of many Scots, and athletics fans generally, in recent years for his no-nonsense, bullish approach on and off the track.

He set out his stall months ago, targeting the men's mile world record - which had stood for 27 years - at London's Diamond League on Saturday.

Kerr didn't just break it, he smashed it by nearly half a second, running a simply sublime three minutes 42.66 seconds.

The Scot now heads to his homeland for his second Games appearance, competing in the Commonwealth Mile in search of his first medal for Team Scotland.

The 28-year-old told BBC Scotland earlier this year that "gold in Scotland is what I grew up thinking about" and you'd be a brave soul to wager against him when he's in this mood.

Men's one mile final: Scotstoun Stadium on Saturday, 1 August.

It's hard to believe Kadeena Cox has not yet competed at a Commonwealth Games.

The para-cyclist, who won gold in athletics and cycling at the 2016 Paralympics in Rio, has missed the last two Commonwealth Games because of injury.

But the 35-year-old, who was a contestant on 'I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here' in 2021 after winning Celebrity Masterchef earlier that year, will be hopeful of cooking up a storm at the ever-rowdy Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome for Team England.

In an expanded para track cycling programme, Cox will compete in the C4-5 event with her sights set on another podium finish.

Cox made the watching world sit up and take notice 10 years ago in Brazil. Sure to be well-backed in Glasgow, it'd be well on brand for the vivacious Cox to star in the Glasgow velodrome.

Women's C4-5 4000m individual pursuit final: Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome on Thursday, 30 July.

When it comes to the Commonwealth Games, names don't get much bigger than Chad le Clos.

The South Africa swimmer is one medal away from becoming the most decorated male athlete in the Games' history. His current haul of 18 - seven gold, four silver and a further seven bronze - is not bad going.

And a whack of them were collected in Glasgow 12 years ago when he equalled the legendary Ian Thorpe's record of seven medals in one Games.

At 34, Le Clos won't compete in as many races this time but is set to be on the blocks for the men's 50m and 100m butterfly events.

He won gold in the 100m butterfly here back in 2014, while he pocketed a bronze in the 50m, but he got a gold in that on the Gold Coast in 2018.

Any medal will do for the man from Durban, and where else than Glasgow, following his remarkable show years ago, than to make history once more.

Men's 50m butterfly final: Tollcross Swimming Centre on Wednesday, 29 July.

Men's 100m butterfly final: Tollcross Swimming Centre on Sunday, 26 July.

This rising superstar is more a 'if you don't know, get to know' athlete.

Remember the name: Seine Stowers.

A junior Commonwealth Games champion, Stowers marked her 18th birthday earlier this year with four gold medals - breaking 12 records along the way - at the Universal Weightlifting Championship in her homeland of Samoa.

Competing in the women's 77kg - as she will in Glasgow - she lifted 142kg in the clean and jerk category as she established herself as one of Samoa's most exciting medal prospects for years.

Weightlifting runs in the family, too, with her sister, Feagaiga, a gold medal winner in the Gold Coast and a silver medallist in Birmingham four years ago.

Already, though, Seine appears to be taking centre stage.

American Olivia Reeves holds the world record at 77kg in both snatch (123kg) and clean and jerk (155kg), but with Stowers on the scene, who knows for how much longer?

Women's weightlifting (77kg) final: SEC Armadillo on Wednesday, 29 July.

Rhys McClenaghan has done it all.

A European, World, Commonwealth and Olympic champion on the pommel horse, he is undeniably one of the sport's greats, but we've been warned to expect 'Rhys 2.0' in Glasgow.

Northern Ireland's gymnastics golden boy - who secured Ireland's first Olympic gymnastics medal with his gold in Paris two years ago - was forced into a spell on the sidelines last year with a shoulder injury, but he is ready to bring a new routine over to Glasgow.

"The Commonwealth Games is a good chance to show your work in progress. At the Olympic Games, you want to see your finished product," he said.

"It's going to be a work in progress, but hopefully one that is the best in the world too.

"Part of me is striving be like a younger Rhys, but the reality is I'm doing a completely new routine and the rule changes have pushed me into that direction, that's the Rhys 2.0 there."

McClenaghan won gold eight years ago, pipping England's Max Whitlock - who has been forced to withdraw from these Games with injury - before collecting silver in Birmingham four years ago.

He was the first gymnast to complete the Grand Slam and so arrives at these Games as one of Team NI's wise auld heids - despite only being 26 years old.

It's a frightening prospect for the rest of the field. Even more frightening is the fact he's rebooting for version 2.0.

Men's pommel horse final: The Arena on Monday, 27 July.

title: Wilson can bring something 'very special' to Leeds - Ampadu
description: Leeds United captain Ethan Ampadu believes new signing Harry Wilson can bring something "very special" to the team through his contributions in attacking areas.  Ampadu and Wilson are team-mates at international level for Wales and the midfielder was asked by BBC Radio Leeds about whether he helped convince the attacker to make the switch from Fulham to Elland Road.  "I don't think he needed my convincing to join," Ampadu said.
fullText:
Leeds United captain Ethan Ampadu believes new signing Harry Wilson can bring something "very special" to the team through his contributions in attacking areas.

Ampadu and Wilson are team-mates at international level for Wales and the midfielder was asked by BBC Radio Leeds about whether he helped convince the attacker to make the switch from Fulham to Elland Road.

"I don't think he needed my convincing to join," Ampadu said. "I think he knew what an amazing club this is, what a great time he can have here. I like to think my message or two might've aided him in that direction. I think whenever I've spoken to him in the past the Welsh lads on camp have spoken glowingly about Leeds.

"All the conversations he's had with the manager and club have gone in the right direction. Because I know him quite well and I know him on the pitch, I'm grateful that we've got him in.

"I think everyone saw more last year, I think maybe because he was coming to the end of his contract that gets people talking about you in a different way but his quality, his left foot, the way he works for the team, the way he works for himself, I think all Leeds fans are going to appreciate the hard work he does and the goals and assists is very special and what helps results."

Ampadu also touched on how the Leeds team will have to change this coming season after achieving their goal of staying in the Premier League.

"I think you always have to try to adapt," he said. "You always have got to lean on what worked and you've also got to adapt on what you can improve, so I think any way we can do that is going to be done.

"I think collectively as a team we want to improve no matter which way it is, that's why we have pre-season. It's one of the most demanding leagues in the world, so we know the physicality has got to be there again.
